Title: CrowdStrike Expands Falcon Adversary OverWatch Threat Hunting Across AI and Google Cloud
Context: Extending Threat Hunting and MDR to AI As organizations increasingly connect AI systems to sensitive data, applications, and infrastructure, adversaries have new opportunities...
Full Text:
Extending Threat Hunting and MDR to AI

As organizations increasingly connect AI systems to sensitive data, applications, and infrastructure, adversaries have new opportunities to exploit trusted access and legitimate AI capabilities. According to the CrowdStrike 2026 Threat Hunting Report, AI agents triggered 2.5 times more detection leads than human activity, underscoring how AI-driven activity is increasing the volume and velocity of signals threat hunters must assess.

Falcon Adversary OverWatch Cross-Domain now extends 24/7 proactive threat hunting to AI applications and autonomous agent activity monitored by CrowdStrike Falcon Guardian. By combining Falcon Guardian's runtime context with telemetry across the Falcon platform and frontline adversary intelligence, CrowdStrike OverWatch hunters can uncover manipulation, abuse, and emerging adversary tradecraft that automated detections may miss. This broader context helps hunters connect suspicious AI activity to larger intrusions spanning identities, applications, and infrastructure.

In addition to proactive threat hunting for AI applications and agents, CrowdStrike Falcon® Complete for Falcon Guardian extends 24/7 expert-led managed detection and response (MDR) to AI coding assistants and agents monitored by Falcon Guardian. Specialized analysts investigate malicious prompts, suspicious agent behavior, and threats involving AI tools and skills. Using CrowdStrike Agent Graph, analysts connect AI agent activity with downstream endpoint execution to assess the scope of threats and rapidly contain and remediate confirmed attacks.

Together, Falcon Adversary OverWatch and Falcon Complete bring proactive threat hunting and expert-led response to the AI attack surface.

Going Deeper in Google Cloud

Cloud environments remain a critical part of the modern attack surface. eCrime cloud-conscious activity surged 171% year-over-year as adversaries increasingly used stolen credentials, misconfigurations, and legitimate tools to operate across cloud infrastructure, the CrowdStrike 2026 Threat Hunting Report found.

These attacks can be difficult to uncover because adversaries often blend malicious activity with legitimate administrative operations. Threat hunters need access to detailed cloud telemetry, an understanding of adversary techniques, and the context to connect suspicious events.

CrowdStrike is extending Falcon Adversary OverWatch's advanced threat hunting capabilities to Google Cloud, delivering the same depth and precision of telemetry-driven hunting available in Amazon Web Services (AWS) and Microsoft Azure. By hunting directly on underlying cloud telemetry rather than relying solely on product-generated detections, CrowdStrike OverWatch hunters can identify suspicious activity earlier in the attack chain, including service account misuse, privilege escalation, and signs of lateral movement.

With this expansion, Falcon Adversary OverWatch now delivers consistent, telemetry-driven managed threat hunting across AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud. This helps security teams uncover sophisticated threats across multi-cloud environments without managing separate hunting operations for each cloud.

Broader Hunting Coverage in a Single Offering

Falcon Adversary OverWatch analyzes 7 trillion events daily, surfaces more than 14 million detection leads, and delivers over 36,000 high-fidelity customer notifications each year. Backed by CrowdStrike intelligence on more than 290 tracked adversaries across nation-state, eCrime, and hacktivist groups, CrowdStrike OverWatch hunters know how adversaries operate, the techniques they use, and where to find them.

With proactive AI threat hunting and deeper Google Cloud coverage, CrowdStrike is extending Falcon Adversary OverWatch's visibility across the modern attack surface and connecting suspicious activity across domains to uncover and stop adversaries before they achieve their objectives.

Title: GitHub Launches npm Firewall to Block Malicious Packages Before Installation
Context: The feature, which currently supports only npm packages, is available in public preview for all GitHub Enterprise Cloud customers, including data-resident GitHub Enterprise Cloud
Full Text:
GitHub has announced that it's introducing a new package firewall as a preview to block installation of suspicious npm packages during installation time.

"The firewall inspects both metadata requests and package downloads for signs of malicious activity, acting as an install-time policy gate," GitHub said.

The feature, which currently supports only npm packages, is available in public preview for all GitHub Enterprise Cloud customers, including data-resident GitHub Enterprise Cloud.

According to the Microsoft subsidiary, the firewall is placed between endpoints or internal registries and the upstream package repositories so as to deter malware attacks that compromise systems when packages are installed.

This behavior can expose users to severe security risks, especially when artificial intelligence (AI) agents and CI runners automatically install dependencies to complete a task or build without their explicit permission.

The idea is that endpoints like coding agents and CI/CD hosts use the firewall for their requests instead of directly pointing to the public package registries. The firewall then checks package downloads against policy controls such as minimum package age and malware advisories, and blocks downloads that do not meet those policies.

To use the firewall, administrators are required to configure policy controls, such as the ones listed below -

Block known malware by checking against the GitHub Advisory Database for active malware advisories

Block packages based on the severity of vulnerabilities by checking the GitHub Advisory Database for flaws that affect the requested package version. The control defaults to "Critical only" as the severity level that blocks an installation, although users can choose "High or higher," "Medium or higher," or "Any severity."

Block attestation downgrades by comparing attestations for the requested package version with those of earlier versions and stop the download if the requested version does not have an SLSA attestation.

Block newly-introduced install scripts by checking whether the package recently added scripts that run using preinstall or postinstall hooks, which can be abused to steal sensitive data.

Block packages based on a cooldown period that prevents versions that are newer than the configured minimum age from being installed. The value can range from 1 to 365 days. The default value is 1 day. Users can disable it by setting it to 0.

Users who need access to a package that gets blocked erroneously by the firewall can submit an exception request, which can then be approved by enterprise administrators and security managers.

The development comes as Rust 1.100, which is scheduled for release on November 12, 2026, readies to add support for a configurable minimum publish age, allowing security scanners and maintainers time to flag and block malicious crate releases before they can be installed or used by users.

The value, defined via the "global-min-publish-age" option in "cargo/config.toml," allows users to specify a minimum publication age in days or weeks. If left unspecified, a seven-day waiting period is applied by default to skip releases published within that window.

Over the past year, similar waiting periods have been implemented across open-source ecosystems, including npm, Python, Microsoft Visual Studio Code, Ruby, Bun, pnpm, and Yarn, as a way to bolster software supply chain security by reducing the chance that a newly published, unreviewed version is immediately pulled into a build.

Cooldown periods help add friction and slow down attacks in which a bad actor publishes a poisoned version of a popular package after seizing control of a maintainer account, thereby preventing rapid spread through manual or automated installations.

"The tradeoff is that legitimate fixes have to wait, too, unless developers make an exception," Socket said. "Malicious code also doesn't magically become harmless with age. A release that escapes detection can simply outlast the cooldown. The value is in buying researchers, maintainers, and registries time to act before the next dependency update carries an attack further."

Full Text:
New investment model provides organizations greater flexibility to maximize long-term value from their security investments

SUNNYVALE, Calif. – October 28, 2026 – Proofpoint, Inc., a global leader in human and agent cybersecurity, today announced Proofpoint Flex, a new investment model designed to help organizations invest with confidence by making it easier to adapt their security strategy as business needs evolve.

Security priorities rarely stay the same. Organizations continuously face new threats, adopt new technologies, and respond to changing business needs. Yet security investments are often made years in advance. Proofpoint Flex helps customers protect their investment by giving them greater flexibility to evolve over time.

"Customers want confidence that the investments they make today will continue to support the business tomorrow," said Blake Sallé, Chief Revenue Officer at Proofpoint. "Proofpoint Flex gives organizations more choice in how they invest across the Proofpoint platform, helping them adapt to changing priorities while maximizing the value of their investment."

With Proofpoint Flex, qualifying customers can:

Adapt over time by reallocating eligible committed spending across Proofpoint solutions at contract anniversaries.

Adopt new capabilities faster with Flex Credits that help reduce the cost of expanding protection.

Simplify technology transitions with programs designed to reduce cost and complexity.

"As organizations continue to modernize their security programs, they want investment models that provide greater agility alongside strong protection," said Mark Thornberry, Chief Business Officer at GuidePoint Security. "Proofpoint Flex gives customers more flexibility in how they plan for future security needs, helping reduce friction as priorities shift and new technologies emerge. It's an approach that aligns well with how enterprises increasingly want to manage long-term technology investments."

"Cybersecurity strategies are constantly evolving as organizations adopt AI, address new threats, and navigate changing business priorities," said Jared Crawley, Vice President of Security Sales at SHI. "Our customers are looking for partners that can help them adapt without sacrificing the value of previous investments. Proofpoint Flex reflects that reality by providing a more flexible way for organizations to evolve their security programs over time. This resonates with our customers, and we will invest in tools and resources that help them maximize the value of these agreements and realize the full potential of their Proofpoint investment."

Proofpoint Flex is part of the company's commitment to helping customers get the most value from their security investments, today and in the future. By making it easier to evolve their protection over time, organizations can respond to changing priorities without losing momentum.

Proofpoint Flex is available immediately for qualifying enterprise customers. For more information, visit www.proofpoint.com/flex.

About Proofpoint, Inc.

Proofpoint, Inc. is a global leader in human and agent cybersecurity, securing how people, data, and AI agents connect across email, cloud, and collaboration tools. Proofpoint is a trusted partner to over 80 of the Fortune 100, over 14,000 large enterprises, and millions of smaller organizations in stopping threats, preventing data loss, and building resilience across people and AI workflows. Proofpoint’s collaboration, data and AI security platform helps organizations of all sizes protect their people, defend their data, and adopt AI securely and confidently. Title: Introducing Route 53 Resolved IP Validation for AWS Network Firewall
Context: A supported deployment model – The feature works with distributed deployments, including multiple firewall endpoints, where clients reach a firewall endpoint in their own...
Full Text:
Your workloads reach most destinations by domain name, but a firewall can only act on what it sees in the traffic. For HTTP and HTTPS, AWS Network Firewall domain rules match the name that the client puts in the request, and the client chooses that name. The connections for protocols such as SSH and SSH File Transfer Protocol (SFTP) don’t carry the domain name. The client uses the name only for the DNS lookup and then connects straight to the IP address that DNS returned. As a result, Network Firewall rules for these protocols have used IP addresses, which change over time. For web and non-web traffic alike, Network Firewall had no view of the answers that your DNS resolver returned, because that shared visibility between DNS and the firewall didn’t exist.

On October 21, 2026, we launched Route 53 Resolved IP Validation for AWS Network Firewall, at no additional charge. Amazon Route 53 Resolver now shares the IP addresses that it returns for each domain name with Network Firewall, and Network Firewall checks each new outbound connection against them. With this launch, you can now filter non-web traffic by domain name, and you can prevent Server Name Indication (SNI) manipulation on TLS traffic without needing to enable TLS inspection.

In this post, we explain how the feature works, show how to turn it on in alert mode, and walk through two common use cases. They’re examples; the same check applies to any outbound traffic that you control by domain name.

How it works

Amazon Route 53 Resolver answers DNS queries from resources in your virtual private cloud (VPC) configured to use it, and it’s available by default in every VPC. With this feature, Route 53 Resolver keeps the IP addresses that it returns for each domain name in a resolved IP cache. When a new outbound connection starts, Network Firewall checks the destination address against that cache.

The workload asks Route 53 Resolver at 10.0.0.2 for files.partner.example.com.

DNS Firewall checks the query first. Domain rules can block or alert on it; an empty rule group lets it through.

Route 53 Resolver answers 203.0.113.10 and records the answer in the resolved IP cache.

The SFTP connection to 203.0.113.10 on port 22 reaches the Network Firewall endpoint.

The policy checks the first packet. The address is in the cache, so the connection continues.

The stateful rule passes it, because Route 53 Resolver returned the address for files.partner.example.com.

The connection leaves through the NAT gateway and internet gateway.

The flow log and alert log record the new fields.

The feature has three parts:

An Amazon Route 53 Resolver DNS Firewall rule group – It defines the scope. The answers that Route 53 Resolver returns in every VPC associated with this rule group go into the resolved IP cache. The rule group can be empty. Add rules to it and the same rule group also filters the DNS queries themselves, for example, by blocking lookups of known threat domains. Together, DNS Firewall checks the lookup and Network Firewall checks the connection that follows.

The Network Firewall policy setting – On the first packet of each new connection, before your stateful rules run, Network Firewall checks whether Route 53 Resolver returned the destination address for a domain name. If it did, the connection continues to your stateful rules. If it didn’t, Network Firewall applies the action you chose: Alert, Drop, or Reject.

Resolved-domain rules – In your stateful rule groups, these rules match a connection by the domain name that its destination address was resolved for, so they work with every protocol. Use the name that your clients look up.

The following diagram shows this architecture.

Figure 1. How Network Firewall checks the SFTP connection from use case 1 against the answers that Route 53 Resolver returned

The policy setting checks every connection, not only web traffic. A connection to an IP address that no client looked up through Route 53 Resolver, such as a hardcoded address, fails the check. If any of your workloads connect straight to IP addresses, add those addresses to Bypass destination validation IP ranges before you enforce. A stateful pass rule doesn’t exempt them because the policy check runs before your rules. The check is per address: when any client in an associated VPC looks up a name, its addresses pass the check for every client in scope in the same Availability Zone. For details, see Resolved IP validation in AWS Network Firewall in the AWS Network Firewall Developer Guide.

Prerequisites

To follow along, you need:

DNS through Amazon Route 53 Resolver – Network Firewall can check only answers that Route 53 Resolver returned. Queries that reach Route 53 Resolver through Resolver endpoints or Resolver forwarding rules count.

A Route 53 Resolver DNS Firewall rule group associated with the VPCs whose DNS answers Network Firewall should check connections against.

The policy setting turned on before you add resolved-domain rules – Rules that use domain filtering (the aws_route_53_resolved_domain keyword) need Route 53 Resolved IP Validation turned on in the same firewall policy. Turn the setting on first, in alert mode, then add the rules.

A supported deployment model – The feature works with distributed deployments, including multiple firewall endpoints, where clients reach a firewall endpoint in their own Availability Zone, and with centralized deployments where the firewall is attached natively to AWS Transit Gateway. If routing sends a client to a firewall endpoint in another Availability Zone, its connections fail the check. To move a centralized deployment to a natively attached firewall, see Why and how to migrate to a Transit Gateway attached AWS Network Firewall.

How to turn it on in alert mode

Start in alert mode because clients cache DNS answers. Network Firewall recognizes only the answers that Route 53 Resolver returns after the DNS Firewall rule group is associated with the VPC and selected in the policy. A client that still uses an answer it cached earlier fails the check until it looks up the name again, usually when its cached record expires. Alert mode lets you see this without blocking anything. Allow about 24 hours in alert mode for clients to refresh their caches.

Create a DNS Firewall rule group (it can be empty) and associate it with the VPCs whose DNS answers Network Firewall should check connections against. For the steps, see Creating a rule group and rules.

Or, to use a DNS Firewall rule group that you already have, make sure it’s associated with those VPCs and only those. An answer returned in any associated VPC is valid for every client that the firewall checks. Which clients are checked is set by source IP ranges in step 6.

In the Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (Amazon VPC) console, under Network Firewall, choose Firewall policies, then choose the policy that your firewall uses. On the Traffic inspection tab, in the Route 53 Resolved IP validation section, choose Edit and select Enable Route 53 Resolved IP validation.

For Action, choose Alert. For DNS Firewall rule group, choose the rule group from step 1 or 2.

For DNS expiry exception policy, choose what happens to a connection that’s already open when its entry expires from the resolved IP cache. Continue keeps it running, Drop stops it silently, and Reject stops it with a TCP reset. We recommend Continue so that long-running sessions, such as file transfers, aren’t cut off midway. However, choose the option that fits your security requirements.

For source IP ranges, list the clients to check. If you don’t set it, Network Firewall checks clients in the firewall’s VPC and in any additional VPCs attached to the firewall. If your clients are in other VPCs, such as spoke VPCs that send traffic to a firewall attached to a transit gateway, enter their CIDR ranges; otherwise, Network Firewall doesn’t check their connections. Add destinations that you allow by IP address to Bypass destination validation IP ranges. Choose Save.

The following screenshot illustrates these steps.

Figure 2. Route 53 Resolved IP Validation turned on in alert mode

In alert mode, Network Firewall doesn’t block a connection that fails the check, and it doesn’t write an alert of its own. It records the result in your flow logs, in the route53_resolved_ip field of each connection. A value of true means Route 53 Resolver returned the destination address for a domain name. A value of false means it didn’t, so enforcement would block the connection. The same field also appears in alert log records that a rule or the policy’s default action writes for the connection. Pass rules don’t write one unless they have the alert; keyword. The DnsUnresolvedFlows metric in Amazon CloudWatch counts the connections that fail the check, and DnsAzUnavailableFlows counts connections from an Availability Zone that doesn’t support the feature. The following alert log record (trimmed, with example values) was written by a default action that alerts, for a connection to an address that Route 53 Resolver returned:

{ "firewall_name": "egress-firewall", "availability_zone": "us-east-1a", "event": { "event_type": "alert", "src_ip": "10.0.1.10", "dest_ip": "203.0.113.10", "dest_port": 123, "proto": "UDP", "app_proto": "ntp", "route53_resolved_ip": true, "verdict": { "action": "alert" }, "alert": { "action": "allowed", "signature_id": 3, "signature": "aws:alert_established action" } } }

In alert mode, this record is for a TLS connection that presented an allowed domain name but went to an address that Route 53 Resolver didn’t return for it, blocked by the policy’s default action in use case 2:

{ "firewall_name": "egress-firewall", "availability_zone": "us-east-1a", "event": { "event_type": "alert", "src_ip": "10.0.1.10", "dest_ip": "198.51.100.7", "dest_port": 443, "proto": "TCP", "app_proto": "tls", "tls": { "sni": "api.partner.example.com" }, "route53_resolved_ip": false, "verdict": { "action": "drop" }, "alert": { "action": "blocked", "signature": "aws:alert_established_app_layer_to_server action" } } }

Before you switch Action to Drop or Reject, check that connections that fail the check are ones you expect and that destinations you allow by IP address are in the bypass ranges. Reject sends a TCP reset, so a blocked TCP client fails right away instead of waiting for a timeout. After you enforce, blocked connections appear in your flow logs with route53_resolved_ip as false, not in your alert logs. For the metrics and log fields to watch, see Monitoring and troubleshooting resolved IP validation.

Use case 1: Filter non-web traffic by domain name

Before this launch, Network Firewall rules for protocols that carry no domain name, such as SFTP, used IP addresses. Now, you can allow them by domain name. In this example, a workload sends files over SFTP to a partner at files.partner.example.com on TCP port 22, and the partner can change the addresses behind that name at any time. The same approach works for SSH, MySQL, and other non-web protocols. You create it as a standard stateful rule. Follow these steps:

Under Network Firewall, choose Network Firewall rule groups, then choose Create rule group. Choose Stateful rule group and Standard stateful rule, and choose the rule evaluation order that your policy uses.

Choose Add rule. For Protocol, choose TCP. For Destination port, enter 22. Under Domain filtering, enter files.partner.example.com. For Action, choose Pass.

Create the rule group, then add it to your firewall policy.

Figure 3. A pass rule for SFTP on TCP port 22, scoped to the partner’s domain name

If you manage rules as code, the equivalent Suricata rule is shown in the following code. It adds the alert; keyword so that the firewall logs allowed connections. The console rule doesn’t add it.

pass tcp any any -> any 22 (alert; msg:"Allow TCP/22 to files.partner.example.com"; aws_route_53_resolved_domain:"files.partner.example.com"; sid:1;)

When the partner moves its server to a new address, the next DNS answer adds it to the resolved IP cache. There’s no IP list to maintain. The cache keeps earlier answers for longer than their DNS time to live (TTL), so the old address can still pass for a while.

Use case 2: Prevent SNI spoofing without TLS inspection

With SNI spoofing, a client presents an allowed domain name in its TLS request while it connects to a different server. Preventing that has required TLS inspection, which decrypts the traffic. Route 53 Resolved IP Validation prevents it without TLS inspection. In this example, a workload calls a partner API at api.partner.example.com over HTTPS. TLS traffic on port 443 must reach only the addresses that Route 53 Resolver returned for that name. You create a pass rule in a standard stateful rule group, as in use case 1, and the firewall policy’s default action drops everything that no rule passes. Follow these steps:

Under Network Firewall, choose Network Firewall rule groups, and then choose Create rule group. Choose Stateful rule group and Standard stateful rule, then choose Strict order.

Choose Add rule. For Protocol, choose TLS. For Destination port, enter 443. Under Domain filtering, enter api.partner.example.com. For Action, choose Pass.

Create the rule group, then add it to your firewall policy.

In the firewall policy, use strict rule order. For the stateful default actions, choose Application drop established (server-directed only) and Application alert established (server-directed only). The alert action logs what the drop action blocks. For why we recommend these default actions, see Firewall policy configuration in the AWS Security Services Best Practices guide.

Figure 4. A pass rule for TLS on port 443, scoped to the partner’s domain name

If you manage rules as code, the equivalent Suricata rule is:

pass tls any any -> any 443 (aws_route_53_resolved_domain:"api.partner.example.com"; sid:2;)

The pass rule matches the destination address, not the name in the TLS request. TLS traffic on port 443 passes only when Route 53 Resolver returned the destination address for api.partner.example.com. If the partner’s addresses also serve other domain names, such as behind a content delivery network (CDN), those names pass too. To also require the partner’s name in the TLS request, add an exact SNI match to the same rule: tls.sni; content:"api.partner.example.com"; startswith; endswith; nocase;.

Without startswith and endswith, the content match accepts any SNI that contains the name.

A connection that presents the partner’s name but goes to another address doesn’t match the pass rule. If Route 53 Resolver never returned that address, the policy setting’s enforcement action blocks the connection before your rules run. In alert mode, the policy setting lets the connection through to your rules instead, and the stateful default action drops it because the pass rule doesn’t match. Its alert log record shows route53_resolved_ip as false, as in the second example previously. If Route 53 Resolver returned the address for a different domain name, the connection passes the policy check. The stateful default action then drops it because the pass rule doesn’t match, and that record shows route53_resolved_ip as true.

Best practices

We recommend that you follow these best practices:

Keep DNS on Route 53 Resolver – Block outbound UDP and TCP port 53 DNS to other resolvers, including DNS over HTTPS (DoH) and DNS over TLS (DoT), on Network Firewall, so that clients don’t bypass the check. Route 53 Resolved IP Validation alone doesn’t do this. If any client looks up a public resolver’s name, such as dns.google, that resolver’s addresses pass the check.

Keep DNS Firewall rules in those VPCs – Route 53 Resolved IP Validation checks the connections that follow a DNS lookup, not the DNS queries themselves. DNS Firewall blocks lookups of known threat domains with AWS managed domain lists, and its advanced rule groups detect data leaving through DNS queries, such as DNS tunneling.

Start small – Add domain filtering to a few rules at a time, then add more when the results look clean. For domain allow list patterns, see Allow rules and domain allowlisting.

Turn on flow and alert logging and detailed monitoring – Connections that fail the resolved IP check show in your flow logs (route53_resolved_ip: false) and in the DnsUnresolvedFlows metric, not in your alert logs. Pass rules without the alert; keyword don’t write an alert log record.

Pricing and availability

Route 53 Resolved IP Validation is available today in all commercial AWS Regions (Regions other than the AWS GovCloud (US) Regions and the China Regions) where AWS Network Firewall and Amazon Route 53 Resolver DNS Firewall are available, at no additional charge. For the list of Regions, see AWS Capabilities by Region. A DNS Firewall rule group with no rules doesn’t incur DNS Firewall charges. Standard DNS Firewall pricing applies after you add rules. See AWS Network Firewall pricing and Amazon Route 53 pricing.

Conclusion

In this post, we showed you how Route 53 Resolved IP Validation works and how to turn it on in alert mode. Network Firewall now checks each connection’s destination against the IP addresses that Amazon Route 53 Resolver returned for the DNS query. Filtering SFTP, SSH, database, and other non-web traffic by domain name and preventing SNI spoofing without TLS inspection are two common examples of what that makes possible. To get started, turn the feature on in alert mode and review the results before you enforce. For the full walkthrough, see Getting started with resolved IP validation.

To learn more, visit the AWS Network Firewall product page and the feature documentation.

Title: ISC2 Launches Cyber-AI Workforce Coalition to Address the Future of AI Security Jobs
Context: Attackers Hide Malware Behind Signed ChatGPT and Claude Binaries Attackers Exploit Teams External Chat to Breach Organizations in Under 15 Minutes Online Scam Volumes Double to...
Full Text:
After years of tracking the global cybersecurity skills gap through its annual Cybersecurity Workforce Study, ISC2 is taking a more active role in shaping the future of the profession with the launch of its Cyber-AI Workforce Coalition.

Announced on October 20, the new coalition is one of the first major developments introduced by Scott Beale, ISC2’s CEO, who took on the role in December 2025.

Speaking to Infosecurity during the ISC2 Security Congress 2026, in Denver, Colorado, on October 26, Beale said he spent his first six months as CEO listening to the organization’s members.

A key finding from the consultation was that a majority of ISC2 members want the nonprofit to more ambitiously and vocally step into the AI safety and security space.

“We want to be the association that can help prepare the cybersecurity workforce for the many challenges of this AI era,” Beale added.

Mapping the AI Security Workforce and Its Emerging Skills Gap

Beale described the coalition as a “vendor-neutral convener” for global cybersecurity professionals. It aims to include thought leaders like HR managers and CISOs, some of the largest employers of cybersecurity practitioners, standard-setting bodies and even government representatives to discuss how cybersecurity roles are changing because of AI.

“Even as the US National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) and others are updating standards and frameworks, companies are still facing a lack of resources for how to best advertise and fill these roles. How a bank describes these jobs is still very different from how a hospital would,” Beale said.

Hiring needs at the intersection of AI and cybersecurity remain uncertain, according to Beale. There remain unanswered questions about how AI will affect future demand for cybersecurity professionals, which skills will be most critical for AI security roles, and how experienced practitioners can upskill to meet emerging demands.

“The coalition a way for us to listen directly to these people and help move the sector in a way that can be responsive to their needs,” he said.

Practical Tools to Define and Hire for AI Security Roles

In practice, the coalition will not create new standards or frameworks but will instead focus on delivering toolkits for employers to help them describe new job roles at the intersection of AI and cybersecurity.

These toolkits will include guidance for how employers hire, develop and organize cybersecurity talent, and how practitioners can identify and build the expertise employers need.

These new tools will help answer three main questions:

How are cybersecurity jobs changing?

How are employers writing job descriptions for these new roles?

How are candidates preparing to interview and fill these jobs?

“As you know, ISC2 is working on a new AI security certification, and certainly we think It is going to be part of that answer and will help us define some of these new roles,” he said. “However, by no means do we pretend having the only solution to this problem.”

The coalition will hold its first meeting in November. Beale hopes it can develop its first series of toolkits by the spring of 2027 and have some companies using them in a pilot phase to help them hire AI security professionals.

The tools produced by the coalition are expected to eventually be made available for everyone to use, not just ISC2 members. Beale believes they will also be useful for universities and certification bodies to adapt their curriculums.

Title: Introducing the Cloudflare PHP Capture the Flag challenge
Context: We shipped client updates and multiple mitigations, updated our web application firewall (WAF) with new rules to block attackers from exploiting the PHP vulnerabilities, and...
Full Text:
Last week was one for the Internet security history books. First, eight eMudhra intermediate certificates were compromised, creating the possibility of forged certificates that could be used to impersonate servers. Then came php2shell: serious vulnerabilities in PHP, the runtime behind a large portion of the Web.

Cloudflare worked around the clock as these events unfolded to protect our customers and help protect the Internet. We shipped client updates and multiple mitigations, updated our web application firewall (WAF) with new rules to block attackers from exploiting the PHP vulnerabilities, and introduced a new feature called full transaction detection.

As always in situations like this, these new capabilities were made available on all plans, including Free.

Put our WAF to the test

Protecting systems from vulnerabilities like these is always an ongoing process, not a one-time event. The widespread adoption of AI allows attackers to discover new vectors with unprecedented speed and efficiency, so collecting real-world data to test our assumptions and strengthen defenses is essential.

That’s why today we're launching the Cloudflare PHP Capture the Flag challenge, run through our Bug Bounty program. We've put a deliberately vulnerable PHP installation behind our WAF, and we're inviting security researchers on HackerOne to try to bypass the protections and capture a flag.

How this Capture the Flag (CTF) works

We are keeping this simple. The challenge focuses on CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, the two PHP vulnerabilities behind php2shell. The target runs stock PHP 8.5.11 (with standard PHP extensions), Apache 2 (via mod_php), and an empty index.php inside a Cloudflare Container, with our default WAF protection rules for these vulnerabilities enabled in front of it. Inside the sandbox is a file called /flag.

The sandbox is reset every few minutes, including the flag file.

Your mission, should you choose to accept it: bypass the WAF protections, exploit the PHP sandbox, and recover the contents of /flag. You can use your own research tools. The challenge page has the environment details, scope, and flag verification form.

Challenge requirements

This limited-time challenge is run via Cloudflare's Bug Bounty program on HackerOne. All aspects of this challenge are subject to HackerOne terms and the Cloudflare HackerOne program rules the (“Bounty Terms”). If you find an eligible bypass, you must follow these requirements in order to claim the bounty:

All participants must sign up for a HackerOne account and review and agree to the Bounty Terms before participating in the CTF.

Demonstrate attacker-controlled PHP code or command execution inside the sandbox through an authorized POST request.

Use that remote code execution (RCE) to recover the current contents of /flag, then successfully verify the flag through the CTF user interface (UI). Verify promptly before a reset; retain the successful result for later review.

Submit a private report to Cloudflare on HackerOne. Include PHP CTF in the title and provide:

The endpoint, complete payload, and request sequence, preserving relevant headers, encoding, and body bytes.

Raw request/response captures or a readable proof of concept sufficient to reproduce the full chain.

An explanation of the WAF bypass, executed code or command, and how that execution recovered /flag.

The attempt ID, successful UI verification result, and exploit/verification UTC timestamps. Include the flag privately if needed for verification.

What makes the method or payload materially distinct, and related submissions you know about.

UI verification does not submit a HackerOne report or establish reporting priority. File disclosure without RCE, RCE without successful flag recovery and UI verification, local-only exploits, rediscovery of the known PHP vulnerabilities, and WAF detection differences or partial chains without the full objective are not eligible.

Awards require a materially distinct Firewall (WAF) bypass method, even for the same PHP CVE. Reports using the same Firewall-bypass mechanism are duplicates, regardless of differences in the PHP exploit, payload, RCE technique, or flag-recovery method. New flags, resets, attempt IDs, or cosmetic changes—including equivalent encodings—do not qualify as unique. Equivalent submissions are duplicates even if unfixed; only the first complete, reproducible HackerOne report is considered. Cloudflare makes final duplicate and reward decisions.

We record attempted metadata and request payloads to help analyze reports, so please use test data only. Do not send credentials, personal information, or anything else you would not want included in a research record. Read Cloudflare’s privacy notice before testing.

Testing is authorized only against the challenge hostname's WAF-protected /php/* endpoints (POST method only). Other Cloudflare services, direct access to the underlying infrastructure, the upstream PHP project, and third-party systems are out of scope. No denial of service, high-volume scanning, persistence, social engineering, or attacks on other participants. If you get a 429 or 503, back off.

In the event of any conflict between this blog post and the Bounty Terms, the Bounty Terms shall prevail.

Cloudflare reserves the right to suspend or terminate this challenge at any time. Once the competition is removed from HackerOne, it is officially terminated, so please refer to the Cloudflare HackerOne page for the most up-to-date information on whether this challenge remains open.

Not a substitute for patching

Our WAF protects you, but it is not a replacement for fixing vulnerable software. Response blocking can prevent exposed data from reaching an attacker, but it cannot undo actions already performed at the origin. If you run PHP, follow the latest PHP security advisories and apply the relevant updates.

Last week was a reminder that helping build a better Internet often takes many people—researchers, maintainers, and teams across the industry—doing difficult, urgent work together.

We hope this challenge gives everyone a useful way to join in. Head over to php-rce.cloudflare.app if you want to participate: the flag is there, and we'd like to know if you can get it.

Title: Cloudflare Introduces a Faster TypeScript Compiler Written in Rust
Context: Cloudflare announced on October 20 that it is bringing tsrs, a Rust port of the TypeScript compiler, into its Oxc toolchain
Full Text:
Microsoft’s Go port of TypeScript’s compiler and tooling delivered roughly 10× faster type checking. Now Cloudflare is working on a Rust port of TypeScript’s compiler that promises even faster type checking and lower memory use. The TypeScript team is collaborating on the work, and some of the optimizations are already making their way into the official compiler.

Cloudflare announced on October 20 that it is bringing tsrs, a Rust port of the TypeScript compiler, into its Oxc toolchain. Its VoidZero team is taking on development and maintenance.

The project began with Max Schwenk, head of AI developer experience at Owner.com, a company that makes software for restaurants. Type checking its large TypeScript backend was consuming enough time and memory to make running several coding agents on a laptop impractical. Schwenk used Claude coding agents to build the initial Rust port, then tested and optimized it against the Go compiler before moving the project to Oxc.

For VoidZero, which Cloudflare acquired in June, this extends years of work on JavaScript tools written in Rust. Its projects include the Oxc parser and compiler tools, the Rolldown bundler, the Oxlint linter, and the Oxfmt formatter. A TypeScript compiler fits naturally alongside that work and could supply the type information needed by tools such as Oxlint.

The Oxc team has already begun refactoring tsrs to improve performance, memory usage, and maintainability. Schwenk says the team cut two releases on its first day. Some optimizations discovered in tsrs have also made their way back into the official TypeScript compiler.

The compiler race has moved beyond Microsoft’s Go port

Microsoft announced its native Go port in March 2025, promising roughly a tenfold performance improvement over the JavaScript implementation. Now other teams are porting that implementation again.

Bun introduced bun check on October 10, reporting type checking 3× to 6.4× faster than TypeScript 7.0.2 in its benchmarks. It ports the Go compiler and checks types without emitting JavaScript or providing an editor language server. Theo Browne’s tsc-rs, another Rust port of TypeScript’s compiler, is being merged with tsrs. Vercel Labs has even ported the Go compiler back into TypeScript, then compiled it to native code with scriptc.

AI coding agents have also changed how long a project like this takes. Cloudflare says current models can carry out large-scale ports almost independently in days. Peter Steinberger contrasted that with the time Microsoft spent on its Go port:

tsrs reports faster checks with substantially less memory #

Cloudflare reports that tsrs is up to 8× faster and uses approximately 70% less memory than TypeScript 7.0 with the same number of type checking workers.

The company also addresses the competing benchmark claims directly. Different machine sizes and compiler settings can produce very different results, it says, and it worked with the TypeScript team to compare equivalent configurations. The benchmark tooling and methodology are public.

Those figures describe the matched configuration. By default, tsrs adapts to the machine it runs on, trading some additional memory for faster checking.

tsrs started with a resource problem at Owner.com. Its backend has approximately 37,000 TypeScript files checked as one program. Schwenk reports that a single-threaded check with TypeScript 7.0 took 80 seconds and 19 GiB of memory. Add linting, development servers, and several coding agents, and even well-equipped laptops were running out of room.

Early users are reporting improvements on their own projects. Kevin Kern tried it on an application with approximately 190,000 lines of code, calling the results promising.

When several agents are working in separate worktrees, type checking can eat up CPU and memory several times over. Cutting that overhead makes room to run more agents at once. That’s part of the appeal for Jimmy Lai, who is considering a move to tsrs for the ChatGPT codebase.

The TypeScript team is already bringing improvements upstream #

The speed claims have prompted questions about why Microsoft should keep investing in the Go implementation. But the TypeScript team is actively involved in understanding and applying the improvements.

TypeScript’s Daniel Rosenwasser said on Hacker News that the team has been working with tsrs’s maintainers to understand its performance and which optimizations are safe. The team has even tried its own Rust port.

Rosenwasser said “a lot of the speed does not just come down to language choice.” Some improvements discovered in tsrs are contributing to a faster, leaner TypeScript 7.1, and the team will continue improving the official tools.

Cloudflare’s announcement puts TypeScript 7.1 beta at up to 2.5× faster than 7.0. The headline 8× comparison is against 7.0, so it should not be read as an 8× lead over the latest beta.

The Rust ports also build on Microsoft’s existing compiler architecture and test infrastructure. Schwenk’s approach began by preserving the Go implementation’s algorithms and behavior, using TypeScript’s conformance tests to check the result. The team aims to have tsrs behave exactly like the official TypeScript compiler as it evolves.

WebAssembly makes the Rust port useful in more places #

WebAssembly support is another reason Cloudflare wants a Rust implementation.

Go can compile to Wasm, but its garbage collector comes with it. Rust’s memory management avoids bundling that collector and gives developers more direct control over allocation and interaction with the host. Cloudflare sees that as a better fit for development tools running within constrained environments.

The appeal is a complete validation loop that can run close to the code, including inside a browser or a Cloudflare Worker. An agent could edit files and check the result within a sandboxed development environment. A browser-based tool could check a project locally without sending the type checking job to a separate server.

The @tsrs/wasm package already supports checking in-memory project files in browsers, and the project links to a browser playground. The Wasm build currently runs on one thread, does not support watch mode or LSP, and has a maximum of 4 GiB of linear memory per instance.

Oxc gives tsrs a home for continued maintenance #

A fast port needs to keep up with TypeScript’s next release, and the release after that. Cloudflare’s Oxc team is taking on that ongoing work.

They are working with Browne to combine tsc-rs and tsrs into one package, including support for LSP and content mappers. Browne had already expressed doubts about whether he would maintain his separate rewrite. Combining the projects gives that work a path into a compiler with an established tooling team behind it.

Cloudflare intends to use the process it developed for Vinext to track TypeScript: agents review upstream changes, identify compatibility gaps, run upstream tests, and propose fixes. The team is also exploring using tsrs for type-aware lint rules in Oxlint.

AI can produce a compiler port quickly, but that leaves developers wondering who will maintain it once the initial excitement wears off. Amid what VoidZero's Michael Dong calls “slopforks,” tsrs has an established tooling team committing to ongoing compatibility, working with TypeScript’s maintainers, and contributing improvements back.

The team is still working toward a stable release and ironing out differences from the official TypeScript compiler, including the order in which errors are reported. Its maintainers acknowledge remaining differences, including diagnostic ordering. Developers can try the npm package today:

npm install --save-dev tsrs npx tsrs --noEmit

The tsrs maintainers say the TypeScript team will continue to control the language’s design and direction. Their job is to preserve that behavior in Rust and contribute useful improvements upstream. With new compiler ports arriving this quickly, the commitment to keep aligning that work with the TypeScript team is a substantial part of tsrs’s appeal.

Full Text:
PRESS RELEASE

LEAWOOD, Kan. — Oct. 21, 2026 — Optiv, the world’s largest pure-play cybersecurity company, today announced CyberBOT, a free, hands-on cybersecurity learning program designed to help classrooms, nonprofit organizations and communities develop practical skills for recognizing and defending against common cyber threats, helping people stay safer and more confident in a digital, AI-powered world.

“Schools, nonprofits and local organizations play a vital role in strengthening the communities they serve, but cybercriminals don’t discriminate based on an organization’s mission or the people it serves. At the same time, many of these organizations lack the resources to dedicate to cybersecurity,” said Amber Peacher, senior corporate social responsibility manager at Optiv. “CyberBOT helps close that gap by giving educators and community leaders a free, easy-to-use resource to build safer digital habits and strengthen cyber resilience year-round.”

Related:AI Takes Root in Hospital Corridors, Raises Security Stakes

Developed by Optiv’s cyber education team, the CyberBOT program brings cybersecurity concepts to life through five interactive sessions focused on common cyber threats people encounter in their everyday lives and best practices for staying protected:

Cyber Threat Actors: Identify cyber threat actors, motivations, tactics and real-world attack scenarios.

Email Security: Recognize phishing attempts, suspicious messages and email threats.

Password Security: Build stronger passwords and protect accounts from unauthorized access.

Social Media Security: Manage online privacy and reduce exposure to social media threats.

Mobile Security: Protect mobile devices, applications and personal information from threats.

Each session combines hands-on activities with classroom exercises designed to make cybersecurity concepts engaging and memorable. Activities include short stories, posters, group analysis, games and role-playing — giving participants opportunities to apply what they learn in realistic scenarios.

CyberBOT also provides educators and facilitators with a comprehensive Educator Guide, offering everything needed to deliver the program, including workshop themes, activity instructions, timing guidance and printable templates. Educators can also use a downloadable certificate template to recognize students for completing each session and demonstrating a commitment to cybersecurity awareness, digital safety and responsible technology use.

Download the free CyberBOT Educator Guide

“We have been eagerly awaiting this cyber awareness training from Optiv. The more our students know, the safer they will be as they engage online,” said Mary Esselman, CEO of Operation Breakthrough, an organization that provides a safe, loving and educational environment for children in poverty and empowers their families through advocacy, emergency aid and education. “These skills are critical, and they're offered in a format that really captures kids' attention. We offer our teens career exploration in cybersecurity, and Optiv's course will be a great introduction to the field.”

Related:Third Serengeti Sweep Tops 1,400 Arrests as Investigations Mature

Advancing Cyber Education Through Optiv Chips In

CyberBOT is part of Optiv Chips In, Optiv’s community impact initiative dedicated to empowering the next generation of cyber leaders.

Through CyberBOT, Optiv is helping make cybersecurity education more accessible to students and educators while introducing young people to the skills and concepts that can serve as a foundation for future careers in cybersecurity.

For the latest news and updates from Optiv, visit https://www.optiv.com/newsroom.

Title: Introducing full transaction detection for Cloudflare WAF
Context: ref Signature reference IDs, up to 10 The first full transaction detections focus on exploit confirmation for high profile vulnerability
Full Text:
Today, we are expanding our web application firewall (WAF) by adding two new capabilities: full transaction detections and response rules. Full transaction detections evaluate each HTTP request alongside its response to identify evidence of exploitation. It helps answer both "Does this request look malicious?" and "What happened when the application handled it?" Response rules can then block the origin’s response before it reaches the requester.

These are valuable protections because the latest frontier models are uncovering vulnerabilities buried deep in widely used software, giving defenders clarity on what to fix — and attackers new paths to exploit. The recent php2shell vulnerability shows the stakes: a flaw in a common software component can put applications across the Internet at risk. AI agents scanning for vulnerabilities can be extremely persistent, adapting payloads using feedback, and chaining vulnerabilities, credentials, and permissions. An application's response can reveal whether an attempt worked and give an attacker information that helps them go deeper.

Inspecting incoming requests remains essential for stopping recognizable attacks before they reach an application. But some threats become clear only when the request is considered alongside what the origin returns. A suspicious input followed by a response exposing sensitive information tells a different story from the same input followed by a rejection or an error.

With these new capabilities, customers can use Cloudflare-managed protections or build their own policies combining request and response properties. This extends our always-on application security framework, with detection results available in Security Analytics to support investigation. Our first managed protections using this capability address the recently disclosed php2shell vulnerability.

And the best part? We are making these new capabilities generally available to all Cloudflare customers, including Free plans.

Request inspection is not enough

Cloudflare WAF protects websites and APIs with managed rules, custom rules, and rate limiting. Managed rules provide protection for known attack techniques and vulnerabilities while custom rules let teams create their own policies using parameters such as an IP address, URL path, headers, and request body. These controls operate at the request level to stop exploits or unwanted traffic from reaching the origin.

For many threats, this is the right place to act. However, treating every suspicious request as a confirmed exploit creates a difficult choice. Broad request signatures can catch more potential attacks, but they can also show “false positives”, such as matching legitimate traffic — which then breaks the applications. Deploying only rules that do not trigger false positives reduces that risk, but can leave more room for more ambiguous traffic to reach the server.

The response provides the missing evidence. Cloudflare can now correlate it with the request that produced it, so detections can account for the outcome of the entire HTTP transaction.

As an illustrative example, consider an application that lets users download files. An attacker manipulates the file parameter to request a private configuration file outside the permitted directory:

GET /download?file=../../config/database.ini

Request inspection can recognize this path traversal attempt and block it before it reaches the application. The request alone, however, cannot establish whether the application would expose the file. It might reject the request, ignore the traversal, or return an error. If the request reaches the origin, a response like this provides additional evidence:

200 OK Content-Type: text/plain [database] username=app_service password=EXAMPLE_SECRET

Full transaction detection provides a missing piece: it can correlate the attempted file access with response content characteristic of a private configuration file. Configuration-like text can legitimately appear in documentation or example downloads; combining it with a traversal attempt provides stronger evidence of sensitive data exposure than either signal alone. A response rule can then replace the origin response with a Cloudflare WAF block page and HTTP 403 before it reaches the requester, effectively blocking the exploit by preventing sensitive information from reaching the attacker.

Detection and mitigation are separate by design

Full transaction detection extends the always-on detection framework we introduced earlier this year. Detections analyze traffic and attach metadata to the request and response, rules then decide what to do with those results.

Separating those jobs gives customers visibility before they design a policy. Security teams can inspect detections in their own traffic, understand which endpoints and signatures are involved, and choose the response that fits their application. Similar to the approach for the request-based Attack Signature Detection, the outcome of the detections are stored in fields that can be accessed in the response custom rules or used in managed detections to block traffic.

Mirroring the request detection fields, the following new fields are added to our platform:

Field

Description

cf.waf.signature.response.confidence

Confidence values associated with matching signatures

cf.waf.signature.response.categories

Categories associated with matching signatures

cf.waf.signature.response.ref

Signature reference IDs, up to 10

The first full transaction detections focus on exploit confirmation for high profile vulnerability. It correlates suspicious input with response signals that indicate an exploit may have succeeded.

We will expand coverage over time by supporting other use cases, including detecting data exposure and exfiltration signals. This is important for the Internet beyond any one application: defenses can distinguish probing from evidence of impact, while detection of exposed data and services can reach customers that do not have a dedicated security team tuning every WAF rule.

Create rules on the response

Detecting evidence of exploitation is most useful if you can act on it in real time. Response custom rules turn full transaction detections into inline protection by blocking a matching origin response before it reaches the requester, although it cannot undo actions already performed at the origin.

Security teams can now combine request and response properties with detection results to decide which responses to block. When a blocking rule matches, Cloudflare replaces the origin response with a WAF block page or a custom response.

Response phase controls are available in the Cloudflare dashboard at the bottom of the Security > Security Rules page, with both managed protections and custom rules.

We have released both managed and custom rules to all plans, including Free plans. Over time, we will follow the same approach we use for request detections, where managed detections for free plans focus on high-profile vulnerabilities, while paying customers get a richer catalog of detections.

Managed detections

All customers get the protection of the full array of transaction detections through the Cloudflare Managed Response Firewall Default ruleset, which is designed for a simple one-click deploy and simplified configurability. When a signature matches, the managed detection will block the response and return a standard WAF block page.

You can edit the Cloudflare Managed Response Firewall Default scope to run detections only on a portion of their applications, for example by excluding or restricting the detection to a specific path. Paying customers can use detection fields in custom response rules to create more tailored policies.

Custom rules

Custom response rules are designed to give customers full control of the rule logic. A useful rule can stop an administration interface from being exposed when an authentication gateway has not marked the request as internal. For example:

http.request.uri.path starts_with "/admin" and not http.request.headers["x-internal-user"][0] eq "true" and http.response.code eq 200 and http.response.headers["content-type"][0] contains "text/html"

This blocks only when an unauthenticated request targets `/admin` and the origin actually returns a successful HTML administration page. It does not block ordinary authentication failures, redirects, or non-administration traffic.

All customers can create up to three custom response rules supporting Log and Block actions. The fields and functions available in response to custom rules mirrors what your plan gives you access to in request custom rules already. Creating rules on the response body is not yet available.

Following the Attack Signature Detection approach, paying customers also have access to the outcome of attack detections through the cf.waf.signature.response.* fields listed above. These fields can be combined with other parameters (such as a hostname, URL path, source IP, request header) to enable protection on a single path, or limit the policy to application-specific context. We are currently rolling out the response fields to all our accounts. If you don’t have access to them yet, please contact your account team.

Investigating matching requests

When a managed or custom response rule logs or blocks a transaction, the event is available in Security Events. This means responders can trace any detection back to the full context of the request and the specific rule that took action.

At the moment, both request-only rules and full-transaction rules are shown together in the same analytics page. In Security Events, the events generated by response rules are part of the Managed Rules or Custom Rules service. You can filter events belonging to a specific rule ID in the relative rule list section.

Get started today

Full transaction detection is generally available for all zones proxying traffic through Cloudflare. To verify that you’re protected, go to Security > Security Rules in the Cloudflare dashboard. If you want to customize your policy, start by reviewing full transaction detections in Security Analytics, then create the response phase policy that fits your application.

Title: Shadow AI Detection Now Extends to Developer Workstations
Context: ZIP files shared between co-workers containing new agent skills, locally-developed MCP servers passed between developers, and locally stored newly-minted agents are all...
Full Text:
ZIP files shared between co-workers containing new agent skills, locally-developed MCP servers passed between developers, and locally stored newly-minted agents are all seemingly harmless files that are commonly used in corporate software development environments.

Unfortunately, far from being harmless, these locally stored files can contain AI assets that were never detected or registered as an approved artifact in your applications.

Such skills are what we refer to as “Shadow AI,” and often they reside on private developer workstations, which are often not governed by central controls. The good news is that you can now detect “local Shadow AI”. By deploying JFrog AI Security, you can extend Shadow AI detection from your repositories to the laptops and workstations where these coding agents actually run, and the work gets done. Let’s break it down.

Ungated Executables: How AI Assets Bypass Security Controls

Until recently, building software followed a strict, secure process: approved code and tools come from trusted official sources, get scanned for vulnerabilities, and must pass company security policies before anyone is allowed to use them.

In today’s “AI-Era”, you can no longer rely on this traditional process for AI assets. Because AI tools and developers can instantly introduce unvetted files, scripts, and plugins on-demand – often straight from GitHub, Slack threads, or even generated by the agent itself – these assets completely bypass standard security checks. This turns a controlled, predictable workflow into something instant, random, and unmonitored.

Some examples include:

Skills: bundles of instructions and scripts that define how an agent performs a task.

MCP servers: Model Context Protocol servers, the connectors that enable agents to interact with systems such as databases, Jira, or Slack.

Plugins: installable packages that bundle skills, MCP servers, and more.

All of these unchecked assets represent serious potential security issues. Perhaps this is best exemplified by Hooks, where authors single-handedly decide what runs on which machine every time the agent is invoked – without ever consulting the rest of the team.

In essence, we wind up with two paths: the Managed Path where assets are scanned and vetted, and the Local Path where Shadow AI components go undetected.

Two paths for AI assets: one governed by JFrog, one with no gates and no reviews

Security Beyond the Repo: Protecting Developer Workstations

Previously, JFrog AI Security detected Shadow AI in your software supply chain by scanning AI models in your JFrog Artifactory repositories and calls to external AI services in your builds. That established a baseline for what we detect in the managed path of your software supply chain, and it worked pretty well, until now.

Shadow AI is more challenging to detect than third-party code and open-source packages, which are introduced into the development environment through a well established centralized build process and not stored on local machines.

Previously, the main risks on developer machines were due to extensions or tools over which DevOps had full control. The risk today is that malicious or non-compliant AI assets, used by coding agents, represent a new type of risk happening autonomously without visibility or control over developer laptops and workstations. This requires an added layer of protection that transparently detects Shadow AI on local machines without affecting developer productivity.

In addition to detecting AI assets on developer machines, JFrog AI Security also provides essential information to security teams and platform administrators regarding potential threats, including:

What risk does it carry? A skill that can run shell commands carries much greater risk than one that can only read files.

Is it allowed by organizational policy? A GitHub MCP server on a laptop may be acceptable if it matches the one you approved, but is a problem if someone built it from a random repository. JFrog plans to add this capability in a future release.

Here is how it works in practice:

Detection is enabled by installing the JFrog Agent Plugin on each developer workstation and operates by following these three steps:

Discover. Detects potentially risky skills, MCP servers, plugins, hooks, commands, and monitors.

Scan Locally. Runs a light deterministic rules-based scan on each workstation where the plugin is installed, designed so that the same input gets the same result every time.

Report. Sends metadata, asset identity, findings, and risk analysis to the JFrog Platform.

How Shadow AI assets on developer workstations become visible

Centralized Visibility Across Managed & Unmanaged AI Assets

JFrog AI Security turns detailed AI asset reports into a single unified inventory. Each record shows the asset’s name, type, harness that reported it (Claude Code, Cursor, etc.), number of workstations where it was detected, local risk analysis, JFrog origin, and detection timestamp.

Two key metrics help prioritize the potential threats to address:

Risk Assessment reveals the underlying security findings for each rating upon selection:

Shell Access + WebFetch: High risk of data exfiltration.

Unscoped Write/Edit: Modifies files outside designated directories.

BypassPermissions Mode: Executes actions without required approval.

Origin documents if the asset already exists in the JFrog Platform:

JFrog Artifactory or JFrog Catalog: The selected asset matches an asset already managed by the JFrog Platform.

No Match: The asset does not match any asset managed in your JFrog Platform.

Gain Complete Visibility Over Your AI Assets

Your developers might already be using AI assets that have not been vetted or approved. Detecting Shadow AI on workstations can help you understand the severity and risk associated with each unmanaged AI asset.

JFrog AI Security ensures managed and unmanaged AI assets follow the same rules as every other artifact you ship: one unified supply chain, one system of record with no Shadow AI exceptions.

Title: Introducing ITDR Lookback: Find Out Who Was in Your Microsoft 365 Tenant Before You Were
Context: Today, Huntress Managed ITDR's Lookback feature is generally available for newly onboarded Microsoft 365 tenants
Full Text:
Today, Huntress Managed ITDR's Lookback feature is generally available for newly onboarded Microsoft 365 tenants. Lookback automatically examines up to 180 days of login history to uncover evidence of compromise before Huntress connected. When a compromise is still active, our Security Operations Center (SOC) investigates and revokes the identity's active sessions.

Onboarding a Microsoft 365 tenant feels like a fresh start. You go through your checklist, and a successful connection tells you monitoring has started. But it doesn't tell you if an attacker got there first. Your first day protecting a tenant might be an attacker's twenty-seventh day inside.

That's what Lookback seeks to solve. You get a clearer picture of the tenant you've inherited, plus defenders who act on what they find. And yes, that includes trial tenants.

Six months of login history. A much stronger start.

Lookback runs once, automatically, when a Microsoft 365 tenant finishes onboarding to Managed ITDR. There's nothing extra to configure and no separate scan to remember to launch.

Huntress Managed ITDR's new Lookback feature is generally available, bringing up to 180 days of Microsoft 365 login history into the hunt for existing compromises.

Lookback applies Huntress's full set of Unwanted Access detections to the tenant's available Microsoft 365 login history, looking back up to 180 days. That includes detections for credential theft, token theft, adversary-in-the-middle attacks, suspicious browsers, and datacenter logins.

Here's the tricky part: evidence of an old compromise doesn't necessarily mean an attacker still has access. Someone may have already reset the password or revoked the compromised sessions. Treating every historical finding as a fresh emergency would make onboarding pretty miserable.

Lookback separates findings based on whether the compromise is still active:

Active compromises receive a critical Incident Report investigated by the Huntress AI-centric SOC, with the identity's active sessions revoked. This turns historical evidence into a reason to act right away.

Previously remediated compromises appear in the Identity Security Assessment as historical context. They don't trigger a new incident or an unnecessary lockdown for something you've already fixed.

That distinction matters. A raw list of suspicious logins leaves the sorting to you. Lookback does it first, so you can see what happened and which parts still need attention.

What's in the report, and where do you find it?

Lookback adds a dedicated section to the Identity Security Assessment, covering compromises that predate Huntress monitoring. It shows the period reviewed and previously remediated incidents, including affected identities, relevant dates, and observed remediation evidence, such as a password reset or session revocation. The report gives you a documented history you can use in a customer conversation or share with leadership.

That history sits alongside the assessment's existing coverage of identities, Rogue Apps, Shadow Workflows such as malicious inbox rules, Unwanted Access, and SOC findings and containment actions. Active compromises uncovered by Lookback also receive their own Incident Reports.

Lookback is part of onboarding for newly connected Microsoft 365 tenants. The assessment is generated automatically after onboarding and waits for Lookback to finish, so you receive one complete document. Once that historical review is complete, Managed ITDR continues monitoring for new threats with the Huntress SOC behind it.

The attackers who arrived before we did

In Lookback's first two weeks of early testing, Huntress reviewed more than 400 tenants. Among them were three very different organizations with the same unwelcome surprise: an active compromise already in progress.

A title company and a $2 million wire

A device-code phishing attack gave an adversary access three days before the tenant onboarded. The attacker persisted through a rogue Entra device and was watching a $2 million real estate wire transfer. Lookback surfaced the active compromise, which Huntress contained.

For a business moving that kind of money, "let's wait until the attacker does something else" is a lousy security strategy.

A school district with an unwanted administrator

A school district's Global Admin account had been compromised 27 days before onboarding. An unrevoked refresh token and a rogue Azure AD device kept the attacker's access alive, with the privileges to control the tenant. Lookback uncovered the compromise, and Huntress contained it. Twenty-seven days is a long head start. Connecting a new security tool shouldn't give the attacker more time simply because the break-in happened earlier.

An architecture firm turned into a phishing launchpad

An architecture firm onboarded with a nine-day foothold still active. The attack involved a hidden inbox rule and 103 external OneDrive phishing invitations sent in a single scripted second. The compromised account had become infrastructure for targeting other people. Lookback surfaced the compromise, which Huntress contained.

In all three cases, the attack began before onboarding. Looking backward gave our defenders evidence to act on right away, without waiting for an attacker's next move.

Less guesswork for you, more proof for your customers

If you're an MSP, every new client brings a history you didn't write. You still have to explain what you've inherited and what you plan to do about it.

Lookback helps you start that relationship with evidence from the client's own environment. You can show past compromises, distinguish resolved activity from active threats, and explain where Huntress has intervened. The shareable assessment makes that conversation easier, while SOC investigation and containment keep the historical review from becoming another helpdesk project.

Internal IT teams get the same benefit. Whether you've inherited a tenant through an acquisition, a vendor change, or staff turnover, you don't have to become a Microsoft audit log specialist to spot signs of prior compromise.

And if you're evaluating Huntress, your trial includes the same Lookback protection as a paid tenant. You can see what we find in your environment and how we respond to active threats while you're still making your decision.

Looking back is how we keep moving forward

Lookback is the latest step in our work to build best-in-class Managed ITDR that earns its place in your security stack every day.

The new ITDR dashboard puts identity activity and investigation tools closer at hand, including Rapid Identity Triage, Failed Login Characterization, and Quick SIEM Search. Our standard for innovation is practical: does it help find an attacker, take work off your team, or give you an answer you couldn't easily get before? Lookback delivers on all three, backed by the same 24/7 SOC that protects your identities going forward.
