Title: Trend Micro Announces Up to ¥10 Billion toward Cyber Resilience Initiative to Strengthen Security for Japanese Organizations in the AI Era
Context: The growing threat extends beyond large enterprises and critical infrastructure to smaller businesses, suppliers and service providers that form the foundation of Japan's economy
Full Text:
Initiative supports nationwide modernization of security measures for individuals and small and medium-sized enterprises, with additional access to TrendAI Vision One™ AI security capabilities and expert technical support provided through partners.

TOKYO, Oct. 19, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Trend Micro Incorporated (TSE: 4704) today announced plans for the Japan Cyber Resilience Initiative, a major national effort to help Japanese organizations strengthen their cybersecurity, reduce critical exposures and modernize their defenses for the AI era. This initiative is designed to support not only organizations but also individuals.

Japan's cybersecurity challenge is escalating rapidly. According to threat research from TrendAI™, the global AI security leader and enterprise business unit of Trend Micro, 607 publicly disclosed cybersecurity incidents were recorded during the first nine months of 2026, already exceeding the 594 reported throughout all of 2025*. Furthermore, the growing number of personal data breaches at organizations has exposed sensitive information on a large scale, creating cyber risks not only for enterprises but also for individuals and Japanese society as a whole.

*Cybersecurity incident figures are tallies as of October 9, 2026. Figures may change due to factors such as incidents that are later disclosed retroactively and additional cases being added.

Yet as attacks grow in volume and sophistication, many organizations remain unprepared for the next generation of threats. The growing threat extends beyond large enterprises and critical infrastructure to smaller businesses, suppliers and service providers that form the foundation of Japan's economy.

The program is designed to serve organizations and individuals across Japan, with an initial emphasis on critical infrastructure, major enterprises and the smaller businesses essential to their supply chains. Support will be provided in phases, tailored to organizational needs, eligibility and available resources.

Trend Micro will work closely with its extensive network of channel partners, systems integrators and managed service providers across Japan to extend the initiative's reach. Eligible organizations will receive up to 10 days of professional services free of charge*, delivered through partners to help them access the right cybersecurity expertise and support.

*For details, including requirements for use, please contact us.

Through its enterprise cybersecurity business, TrendAI™, the company proposes to make available up to ¥10 billion in TrendAI Flex licensing credits to help eligible organizations modernize their security environments with TrendAI Vision One™. The initiative also includes plans to mobilize forward-deployed engineers (FDEs) and provide access to managed detection and response (MDR) expertise.

A national challenge demands a national commitment

Japan's senior political leaders have characterized the situation as a cybersecurity emergency.

As a global cybersecurity company headquartered in Japan, Trend Micro has spent decades protecting Japanese businesses while investing extensively in global threat research, vulnerability discovery, threat intelligence and incident response.

"Japan is our home. When the organizations and individuals that power our economy, our infrastructure and our communities face an escalating cybersecurity challenge, we have a responsibility to step forward. No organization should have to face this challenge alone. We are bringing together our technology, our people and our global security expertise to help Japan strengthen its defenses today and prepare for a future in which cyber threats will move faster than ever." said Eva Chen, Trend Micro CEO.

The Japan Cyber Resilience Initiative will provide the following six forms of support to organizations and individuals.

＜For organizations＞

1. Up to ¥10 billion to accelerate cybersecurity modernization

Trend Micro proposes an aggregate allocation of up to ¥10 billion in TrendAI Flex licensing credits to help eligible organizations adopt and expand protection through the TrendAI Vision One™ platform designed to help customers modernize their existing security environments, strengthen protection across critical systems. Through TrendAI Flex Unlimited, customers will also be able to access additional TrendAI Vision One™ capabilities, including AI security innovations.

The initiative will also help existing customers, working with their trusted channel partners where appropriate, build on their current security investments and transition toward modern, AI-era defenses without unnecessarily disrupting established protection.

The proposed allocation represents licensing credits, not a cash grant. The initiative will be introduced in phases, with detailed eligibility criteria, credit allocation and redemption terms, partner participation options, and service availability to be communicated as the program is rolled out.

2. Forward-deployed engineers to turn technology into stronger defenses

Recognizing that cybersecurity modernization requires more than technology alone, TrendAI™ plans to mobilize forward-deployed engineers (FDEs) and technical specialists to work directly with participating organizations.

These specialists will work alongside participating organizations and their existing partners, where appropriate, to assess critical exposures, identify security gaps, prioritize risk reduction and accelerate the deployment of modern security capabilities.

FDE engagements will initially prioritize organizations whose security is particularly important to national infrastructure, economic activity and interconnected supply chains. For smaller organizations, Trend Micro intends to work through appropriate delivery models and its partner ecosystem to help extend the initiative's reach.

3. Expert-led detection, response and operational resilience

Through TrendAI™'s MDR capabilities and security expertise, eligible organizations will be able to explore additional support for continuous threat monitoring, incident investigation and response.

The initiative aims to help organizations move beyond isolated security controls toward a coordinated approach that connects exposure management, threat detection, incident response and proactive risk reduction.

Trend Micro also protects more than 10 million consumers across Japan through its TrendLife™ business unit. Through local partners and a network of managed service provider (MSP) partners serving over 230,000 small and medium-sized businesses, we also help protect close to 2 million business devices. Building on this foundation, we will continue to help strengthen security for consumers and small businesses alike.

4. 60-day free trial of Worry-Free Business Security Services provided (TBD)

Small and medium-sized businesses play a vital role in supply chains, and strengthening their security is increasingly urgent. For these customers, a 60-day free trial of Worry-Free Business Security Services will be provided. In addition, TrendLife™ is considering new support for the Worry-Free series together with its channel partners. Further details will be announced as they are finalized. Note: The free trial is available only to new customers in Japan and must be started by December 31, 2026.

5. Exploring AI-Powered Scam Protection to Strengthen Digital Trust on LINE

As small businesses increasingly rely on LINE Official Accounts (LINE OA) to engage with customers, everyday interactions may also expose them to scams disguised as customer inquiries, suspicious links, or fraudulent requests.

TrendLife™ is advancing API integrations with providers of LINE-related services, enabling AI-powered scam detection capabilities to be seamlessly embedded into customer touchpoints and helping strengthen protection for both businesses and their customers. We are currently working with partners, including Crescendo Lab, one of Asia's leading LINE CRM providers, and are in the final stages of preparation for commercial deployment by the end of the year.

＜For consumers＞

6. 90 days of Trend Micro ScamCheck provided free of charge

TrendLife™ will provide 90 days of complimentary access to Trend Micro ScamCheck, our mobile scam protection app. In the event that leaked personal information is misused in phone, email, or other scam attempts, Trend Micro ScamCheck helps protect users from potential scams.

A lasting commitment to Japan's cyber resilience

Trend Micro will work with customers and partners to translate this initiative into measurable improvements in cybersecurity, with plans to track participation, modernization progress and defensive outcomes.

Organizations and partners interested in participating can contact their Trend Micro representative or visit the Initiative Landing Page to register their interest and receive updates as program details and participation opportunities become available. Title: Huntress + AlgaPSA Integration: Built in Days by Nine Minds
Context: Over the past year, the Huntress API has grown from six read-only endpoints into a full integration and automation platform, along with Webhooks and an MCP server
Full Text:
Over the past year, the Huntress API has grown from six read-only endpoints into a full integration and automation platform, along with Webhooks and an MCP server. For partners, that means Huntress data can show up wherever they already work, not just in our portal. It also means software vendors can build their own Huntress integrations on their own schedule, without having to wait on us.

Nine Minds is a great example. Their team built a Huntress integration for AlgaPSA, their professional services automation (PSA) platform, using our public API documentation. No technical support or special access needed. They just read the docs and, a few days later, had a working integration. This post covers what they built, what the experience was like, and what it shows about how you can use the Huntress API.

Meet Nine Minds and AlgaPSA

Nine Minds was founded by Robert Isaacs and Arnie Bellini, who both spent over a decade at ConnectWise. AlgaPSA is their answer to a problem they saw in the industry for years: PSA tools that are too expensive, too complicated, and primarily built for mature organizations.

AlgaPSA brings ticketing, projects, time tracking, billing, and client operations into one platform, and it was designed with the smallest MSPs in mind. As Robert told ChannelE2E, "The small MSP doesn't want to sign a three-year contract." But as they've progressed, larger MSPs have started taking notice, too.

AlgaPSA gives MSPs control over how they run the software with hosted, self-hosted, and open-source options. Over a hundred MSPs now rely on AlgaPSA for day-to-day operations, with more signing up every week.

Why Build a Huntress Integration?

For Nine Minds, the decision came down to two things. Mutual customers were asking for it, and their team spends a lot of time in the MSP community, including at IT Nation, and Huntress is one of the names they see everywhere.

When your users already rely on Huntress to catch threats, the next question is simple: how do those incidents get to the technicians who need to act on them? The AlgaPSA <> Huntress integration provides an answer.

How the Integration Works

The integration is built around the premise that a security incident should never go without a ticket. When the Huntress SOC publishes an incident report, it appears in AlgaPSA as a ticket on a dedicated security board, with the incident summary and a priority based on its severity.

Technicians work it like any other ticket, and the time they log flows into AlgaPSA's billing and invoicing. That means security responses get tracked and billed like the rest of their work, instead of living in a separate console. When the SOC closes the incident, the ticket can close automatically, too. And if an incident comes from a client that hasn't been mapped yet, it still lands on a triage board, so nothing slips through.

Setup takes a few steps:

Connect your Huntress API credentials

Map Huntress organizations to AlgaPSA clients

Choose where tickets land and how severities translate to priorities.

Nine Minds walks through each step in the AlgaPSA Huntress integration docs.

A few things to know before you start:

Use a dedicated API key. Huntress API keys are tied to a user and mirror that user's permissions, so it's a good idea to create a separate key just for this integration.

You need AlgaPSA's paid tier. The Huntress integration is part of AlgaPSA's Enterprise Edition (also offered as AlgaPSA Pro). It isn't included in the open-source Community Edition.

Finish routing first. AlgaPSA won't start pulling incidents until the security board, the fallback client and board, and priorities for all three Huntress severities (Critical, High, and Low) are set.

Expect tickets on a schedule, not instantly. AlgaPSA checks Huntress for new incident reports at an interval you choose between one and 60 minutes, so tickets show up at the next check.

What Was It Like to Build on the Huntress API?

This is the part we're most excited about. Nine Minds went from idea to a shipped integration in just a few days.

They built it using our public documentation, without reaching out to us first. After a short period working out which data they needed, Robert said things went smoothly: no confusing fields, no missing endpoints, no documentation gaps that slowed them down. Their team also uses AI coding tools, and pointing those tools at the Huntress API docs was enough to get the job done.

"Integrating Huntress into AlgaPSA was easy enough that we almost felt as if we had missed something... [Then] our customers started thanking us for the integration. Working with Huntress could not have been easier."

– Robert IsaacsFounder / CEO, Nine Minds

Nine Minds also built a Huntress emulator so they could test the integration without depending on live incidents. They told us a dedicated sandbox environment would make that easier, and we've shared that feedback with our team.

What Else Can You Build?

AlgaPSA's integration shows one common pattern: pull incidents from Huntress and turn them into tickets. But the API supports a lot more.

A few examples:

Get incidents in real time. Instead of polling, Huntress Webhooks push incidents and escalations to your PSA, Slack, or SIEM as they happen.

Act on incidents. Approve or reject remediations through the Incident Report response API, and isolate or release hosts through the Agents API.

Automate onboarding. Create, update, and delete organizations programmatically. For example, when a new client is added in your RMM, automation can create the matching Huntress organization and start EDR deployment.

Reconcile billing and build reports. Pull billing reports and per-product organization stats, like agent counts, SIEM storage, and ITDR identity counts, into your dashboards, QBRs, or PSA contracts.

Bring Huntress into AI workflows. The Huntress MCP server connects your AI assistant to your incidents, agents, billing data, and more.

Prefer to see how this works? Watch our video below to see inside the Huntress API, Webooks, and MCP server:

Ready to Learn More?

AlgaPSA's integration started with a customer request and ended with a shipped feature just a few days later. That's the kind of experience we want every developer to have with the Huntress API. If you've been thinking about connecting Huntress to your own tools, the docs are a good place to start.

Use Huntress with AlgaPSA: See the AlgaPSA Huntress integration docs for setup steps.

Title: Introducing Evo Agentic AppSec: Security That Keeps Up With AI Development
Context: Attackers are using AI to identify weaknesses, combine lower-severity issues into more serious exploits, and accelerate attacks
Full Text:
AI is changing how software gets built. Coding agents produce more code than teams can review, and current models introduce several times more vulnerabilities per line than human developers. Many of those flaws involve business logic, access control, and authentication, areas where pattern-based scanners have limited visibility.

Most security teams were already behind before any of this started. They are flooded with findings, many of which are noise, while managing a backlog of latent risk. Attackers are using AI to identify weaknesses, combine lower-severity issues into more serious exploits, and accelerate attacks. As of October 2026, Snyk’s data showed roughly eight new vulnerabilities introduced for every one remediated. AI-driven development adds further pressure to that imbalance. And the in-depth security reviews that catch business logic flaws take so much time and context that most teams run them once, for a handful of critical apps.

Software supply chain attacks compound the problem. Malicious packages now account for most open source zero-days, with more than 20 high-profile attacks in 2026 and growth on track to exceed 600% year over year. A malicious package can steal credentials during installation, before a pull request or CI scan runs, and coding agents can introduce these packages without assessing whether they are safe.

Security needs to keep pace with how software is now built and address risks before code reaches review.

The pull request scan is no longer enough on its own

Pull request scanning remains an important control. On its own, however, it cannot address every risk, particularly when code is generated continuously, and malicious dependencies can cause harm before a scan begins.

Application security has to run in three places: checks inside the coding workflow, fast deterministic scans on every change in CI, and deeper analysis of the full application at regular intervals. That analysis must also account for business logic and application context alongside known vulnerability patterns.

Finding more issues is only useful if teams can act on them. Prevention and remediation need to scale too, with clear policies governing what gets blocked, what gets fixed, and what requires human review. Proposed fixes need independent validation before teams accept them.

The answer is not another scanner. It’s the program, run by agents and owned by your team.

Introducing Evo Agentic AppSec

Evo Agentic AppSec is a team of security agents that does the work of your application security program, so your team can focus on setting policy and owning the decisions. It brings these capabilities together to help teams manage application security continuously, from threat assessment and prevention through detection, prioritization, remediation, and verification.

It helps teams assess an application’s threats and controls, identify vulnerabilities, prioritize fixes, and validate the results. The agents work across new code during development, helping to prevent new issues and block the install of malicious packages, and across the applications you have already shipped, so the backlog actually goes down.

Snyk’s security intelligence provides the context behind this work. It combines ten years of deterministic assessments with signals such as reachability, exploitability, breakability, and fix outcomes. That context helps teams separate the issues that matter from the noise, and turns a proposed change into a fix a team can use.

In VulnBump, Snyk’s newest benchmark of real dependency upgrades, Evo Remediation Agent produced mergeable fixes 90% of the time, compared with 59.6% for the same model without Snyk context. A mergeable fix resolves the vulnerability and leaves the project able to build.

Independent verification is central to this approach. Deterministic engines check proposed fixes rather than relying solely on the model that generated them. Teams define the policies and acceptance criteria that govern the process.

Agentic AppSec is the next solution coming to Evo, the part of the Snyk platform built to help teams secure both the applications they develop and the AI agents they deploy.

How it works

Evo Agentic AppSec brings together a team of agents with specific roles:

Evo Agentic Security Review assesses an application’s threats and controls, producing evidence-backed findings and remediation guidance. Now, that depth of review can run across every application, without scaling your team.

Evo Code Scanning Agent identifies business logic and authorization flaws that traditional scanners miss.

Snyk Secrets detects exposed secrets across traditional and AI-assisted development.

Evo Remediation Agent fixes issues in new code and the existing backlog, starting with third-party dependency issues at launch.

Evo Dependency Firewall blocks malicious and out-of-policy packages at install time, before code scanning ever comes into play. You don’t have to tell your agents to be careful about what they install; they pull from trusted packages by default.

Evo Continuous Offensive Security provides adversarial testing to further assess the application’s defenses and the effectiveness of remediation.

Together, these capabilities help teams expand security coverage and handle more remediation work, while keeping a human on the loop, retaining control over policies, priorities, and approvals.

Evo Agentic AppSec builds on Snyk Code and Snyk Open Source. The engines that teams already use to scan code and dependencies provide the underlying analysis and independently validate findings and proposed fixes.

Giving teams more capacity

As more development and security work becomes automated, teams need clear oversight and accountability.

Developers can spend more time reviewing proposed changes. AppSec teams can focus on security policy, exceptions, and the risks that require their judgment. CISOs gain visibility into a continuously running program, with adversarial testing and an audit trail of automated decisions.

For organizations without a dedicated AppSec function, these capabilities can help establish consistent security practices and reduce the manual work needed to maintain them.

The goal is practical: prevent more issues, resolve existing vulnerabilities faster, and give teams evidence that their fixes work.

See it for yourself

Today:

Your backlog is growing faster than it can be burned down

Coding agents keep committing your secrets

Evo Agentic AppSec brings prevention, detection, remediation, and verification to help teams address those challenges.

Full Text:
In November 2015, we released our first in-house macOS sandbox, Box of Apples, followed by an update in March 2018 that introduced HTML behavior reports, desktop screenshots, and process trees. Over the past decade, the macOS ecosystem and the threat landscape targeting it have changed dramatically. Apple transitioned its hardware architecture from Intel (x86_64) to Apple Silicon (ARM64), hardened its operating system security model, and deprecated legacy dynamic tracing mechanisms. At the same time, macOS threat actors have shifted toward native ARM64 binaries, multi-stage social engineering installers, credential-harvesting AppleScripts, and evasive infostealers.

Today, we are excited to introduce macOS Mirage, our brand-new, ground-up dynamic analysis sandbox built natively for Apple Silicon and macOS 26. macOS Mirage replaces Box of Apples as part of the VirusTotal Multi-Sandbox project, delivering high-fidelity behavioral telemetry, automated Sigma behavioral detections mapped to MITRE ATT&CK, and—exclusively within our Private Scanning product offering—full Interactive Live Analysis.

Why We Built macOS Mirage: Beyond Box of Apples

Box of Apples was designed for an era of Intel-based Macs and relied on dtrace scripts to monitor system calls. As macOS evolved, two structural shifts required a completely new approach:

Native Apple Silicon (ARM64) Execution: Modern macOS applications and malware families are compiled natively for Apple Silicon or distributed as Universal Mach-O binaries. Running modern samples on legacy Intel hardware either fails outright or misses architecture-specific execution paths. macOS Mirage runs natively on bare-metal Apple Silicon hardware with Apple's native virtualization stack and macOS 26, ensuring authentic execution fidelity.

Modern Kernel-Backed Behavioral Telemetry: In modern macOS releases, System Integrity Protection (SIP) restricts legacy dtrace hooks, and high syscall volumes could cause event drops. macOS Mirage uses modern, kernel-supported macOS security instrumentation to capture process creation, command-line arguments, file system modifications, persistence installation, and access to sensitive credential stores without losing events.

Multi-mode networking (Internet, Simulated INetSim, HTTPS MITM, Tor, VPN) (Private Scanning exclusive)

Interactive Control

Automated execution only

Live Mouse, Keyboard & Clipboard Control (Private Scanning exclusive)

Rich GUI Execution and Persistence Tracking

Many macOS samples package their payloads inside disk images (.dmg) or application bundles (.app) that initialize graphical windows, register background services, or trigger system notifications during execution. macOS Mirage provides full graphics acceleration and desktop monitoring, capturing both visual screenshots and underlying system modifications in real time.

Figure 1: Dynamic detonation of a macOS application in macOS Mirage, capturing both the application GUI and a macOS system notification alerting to a newly registered persistent background Login Item.

Figure 2: Full window management, 3D rendering, and Dock process tracking inside macOS Mirage.

In addition to capturing screenshots to show what a user would see on screen, macOS Mirage automatically monitors security-sensitive locations across the operating system, including:

Persistence Mechanisms: LaunchAgents, LaunchDaemons, Login Items, and cron jobs.

Shell & Environment Profiles: Modifications to .zshrc, .bashrc, .zshenv, and /etc/profile.

Credential & Privacy Stores: Unauthorized access to Keychain databases (login.keychain-db), browser cookie and credential stores, SSH keys, and the Transparency, Consent, and Control (TCC.db) database.

System & Network Configuration: Changes to /etc/hosts, /etc/resolv.conf, and /private/etc/sudoers.

New Behavioral Detections with Sigma Rules: Catching a macOS Info-Stealer in Action

To help analysts quickly identify malicious behavior without sifting through thousands of raw file and process events, macOS Mirage evaluates runtime telemetry against a curated library of macOS Sigma rules and maps every detection directly to MITRE ATT&CK techniques.

Let's look at a real-world example of a macOS info-stealer and credential-phishing sample analyzed by macOS Mirage on VirusTotal: be77bca22f078d57058535ddcf26a39a752a8df030392cb45ba6a60e06651878

When executed inside macOS Mirage, the binary (unix51436504) performs a multi-stage credential theft and persistence chain:

AppleScript Password Phishing: The malware invokes /usr/bin/osascript to display a deceptive system prompt titled "Password Request" asking the user: "Please enter device password to continue."

Local Credential Validation & LaunchDaemon Persistence: It validates the harvested password against local Directory Services (dscl . authonly) and invokes sudo -S to copy /tmp/daemonplist to /Library/LaunchDaemons/com.somedaemon.plist.

Keychain, Browser & Notes Harvesting: The sample opens the user's Keychain (/Users/admin/Library/Keychains/login.keychain-db), Safari cookies (Cookies.binarycookies), Apple Notes database (NoteStore.sqlite), SSH keys (authorized_keys, known_hosts), and .zsh_history, staging the stolen files under /tmp/lksopo while continuously polling the clipboard via pbpaste.

Secondary Payload Download, Exfiltration & Cleanup: Using ditto, the malware compresses the staging directory into /tmp/lksopo.zip, exfiltrates the archive via an HTTP POST request (curl -X POST), downloads a secondary bot payload (curl -o /tmp/binaryexe), and deletes the staging directory (rm -rf /tmp/lksopo) to cover its tracks.

Figure 3: macOS Mirage screenshot capturing the deceptive AppleScript "Password Request" phishing dialog displayed by sample be77bca22f078d57058535ddcf26a39a752a8df030392cb45ba6a60e06651878.

From this single detonation, macOS Mirage automatically generates a high-confidence malicious verdict (macos_osascript_credential_phishing) and triggers 7 distinct Sigma rules spanning the entire attack lifecycle:

Title: UK Government Announces Sweeping New AI Security Plans
Context: Attackers Hide Malware Behind Signed ChatGPT and Claude Binaries Attackers Exploit Teams External Chat to Breach Organizations in Under 15 Minutes Online Scam Volumes Double to...
Full Text:
The British government has announced a range of new initiatives designed to better protect the nation from emerging AI threats.

Speaking at Imperial College London on October 12, AI minister Kanishka Narayan laid out a series of plans, including the use of frontier models to find vulnerabilities in government systems.

“Our central vulnerability-monitoring service has already helped reduce the time taken to fix identified weaknesses from 50 days to just eight. Built on these advances, I want us to go further,” he explained.

“I am announcing that the DCMS cyber minister, the security minister and I will lead the urgent use of frontier AI capabilities to find weaknesses within government systems before attackers exploit them, protect essential government systems, and respond more effectively to emerging threats.”

This follows a series of internal hackathons run by the Government Cyber Coordination Centre (GC3) where frontier AI was used to find over 400 software flaws in public sector IT which were subsequently patched.

Read more on government AI efforts: UK Government Launches AI Safety Scheme to Tackle Deepfakes.

Narayan also announced that the Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport (DCMS), the National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) and the AI Security Institute (AISI) would work together to “develop robust ways” to respond to and contain agentic AI incidents.

That follows a series of cases in which frontier models have hacked organizations, including governments, during testing.

Additionally, security minister, Dan Jarvis, will lead a “cross-government program to strengthen our defenses against cyber-attacks, including from AI,” Narayan explained.

A National Cyber Action Plan will be published “soon,” he added.

There will also be amendments to the long-awaited Cyber Security and Resilience Bill (CSRB) to help protect organizations from “loss-of-control” risks and AI-powered threats.

“That includes identifying and reporting on serious incidents and near misses, including reducing AI-driven risk across essential services, and ensuring serious AI incidents can be properly reviewed,” Narayan said.

AISI Testing of Frontier Models Resumes

While many of the details related to these initiatives are still being worked out, there was at least confirmation of one positive development from the AI minister.

He revealed that the AISI has resumed testing of frontier models including Gemini 4 Argon, to help better inform model developers and the global community of emerging risks. The Trump administration had previously blocked access to such models by any testing bodies outside the US.

Narayan said that, in the future, the UK could extend this expertise and draw on its heritage in semiconductor design to nurture new capabilities in AI verification. This nascent field will help to ensure AI, and the outputs of models, comply with rules, regulations and safety standards.

Okta field CTO, EMEA, Richard Wainwright, welcomed the focus on AI security and called for kill switches to be considered as part of the CSRB.

“As AI agents become more autonomous, safety must be built into the infrastructure UK businesses and government rely on,” he added. “Everyone wants a 'big red button' to turn off rogue AI agents.”

Carla Baker, senior director of UK policy at Palo Alto Networks, praised the government's focus on proactive threat detection and incident reporting, arguing that adversaries are deploying AI “at scale” in attacks to accelerate intrusions and exfiltration.

"Defense must enable progress, not cause paralysis. Building national resilience isn't about imposing heavy-handed regulation that stifles UK competitiveness,” she continued. “By combining practical, robust security guardrails with the operational agility that organizations need, the UK can safely deploy frontier AI and win on the global stage."

The success of a mandatory incident reporting regime will depend on which organizations it would cover, what counts as “frontier” and how “incidents” are defined, added Manifold Security CEO, Neal Swaelens.

“Given we’re seeing time and time again that incidents of agentic AI breaches are being reported months after they occurred, if mandatory reporting is to have any impact, it must be paired with observability, including proper oversight of what agents are doing at runtime so that incidents can be caught when they happen, and not weeks later,” he argued.

“OpenAI’s agent in Australia's Medicare portal, for example, took months to be detected and disclosed.”

Title: Silverfort Secures AI Agents on Google Cloud in Runtime with Agent Gateway Integration
Context: An expanded collaboration with Google Cloud The Agent Gateway integration is not Silverfort’s only collaboration with Google Cloud
Full Text:
Today, Silverfort announces an integration that brings its runtime Identity Security approach to Agent Gateway, part of Google Cloud Gemini Enterprise, giving teams real-time visibility into AI agent activity and enforcing access decisions as they happen.

After Silverfort was named in Google Cloud’s Next ’26 announcement among the partner services bringing identity and governance administration to Agent Gateway, it is time to announce the new milestone we have been building toward, and it lands at exactly the moment enterprises need it.

A milestone for securing agentic AI

Agent Gateway is a genuinely significant piece of infrastructure. Announced in preview at Google Cloud Next ’26, it provides “an open, extensible, scalable way to enforce centralized governance policies to securely connect agents, models, and tools across runtimes.”

For an Identity Security company, that is exciting news. Every agent interaction can be configured to flow through Agent Gateway, which makes it the natural place to apply Identity Security controls at scale. Silverfort now secures the AI agents running there by connecting directly into the platform’s control plane, so agent owners never have to route traffic through a separate gateway.

Why AI agents change the identity problem

Organizations are adopting AI agents faster than most identity and security teams can inventory, monitor, or control them. These agents authenticate into systems, access sensitive data, and take actions across cloud and SaaS environments, often with broad privileges and limited oversight. The result is a rapidly expanding identity attack surface that traditional security tools were not built to address.

Agents also do not fit neatly into traditional security models. Unlike a human user who logs in once and works within predictable patterns, agents can chain actions across services, escalate broadly privileged credentials and tools, and behave in ways that are difficult to predict or trace. That leaves most organizations unable to answer basic questions: how many agents are running, who owns them, what they can access, and which ones are overprivileged.

These risks also arrive from two directions at once. Alongside the exposure created by an organization’s own agents, adversaries are now using AI-powered attack models built to probe, exploit, and move laterally at machine speed. They are not the same problem, but they converge on one control plane: what an identity is permitted to access, and what it is allowed to do. When agents are overprivileged and attackers are autonomous, the window to act is very small.

What Silverfort delivers on Agent Gateway

Visibility into agent activity

Silverfort automatically discovers AI agents operating through Agent Gateway and maps each one back to its human owner for clear accountability. Security teams get a complete view of agent behavior, ownership, permissions, and access paths across Google Cloud and beyond.

Runtime enforcement controls

Silverfort evaluates agent requests against access policies at the Agent Gateway layer before they reach downstream systems, limiting unauthorized privilege escalation and risky agent overreach. If an agent attempts to access a dataset, SaaS application, or internal resource outside its approved permissions, Silverfort evaluates that request in real time and enforces the appropriate policy response. Unauthorized attempts are stopped in line rather than detected after the fact.

Risk-based prioritization

Not all agents carry the same level of risk. Silverfort analyzes agent exposure based on privilege level, access patterns, and connections to sensitive resources. Overprivileged agents, dormant credentials, and high-risk access paths are flagged and prioritized so teams can focus remediation where it matters most.

Granular access policies and detailed audit trails

Policies are defined by agent identity, target application, and action type, and are managed from a centralized dashboard. Access requests are allowed or blocked in real time, and all agent activity is auditable and tied to enterprise identity governance frameworks and to the human using the agent.

Because the controls sit where agent traffic already flows, organizations gain all of this without deploying additional infrastructure or redesigning how their agents are built. Developers keep building. Agents keep running.

Meeting agents where they actually run

AI agents do not all run the same way, so Silverfort delivers runtime enforcement in two complementary ways. The Silverfort MCP Gateway is a universal inline enforcement layer between agents and the Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers they access, built for custom and open-framework agents operating outside closed, vendor-specific ecosystems.

By connecting directly into the control plane of leading agentic platforms, Silverfort enforces policy without requiring agent owners to route traffic through a separate gateway. That’s the right fit for cloud-managed enterprise environments where scale, platform resilience, and zero workflow disruption are critical.

An expanded collaboration with Google Cloud

The Agent Gateway integration is not Silverfort’s only collaboration with Google Cloud. In June, Silverfort launched an integration with Google Security Operations that pulls live identity risk into SecOps playbooks and pushes enforcement back the other way, letting analysts raise a user’s risk indicator or tighten a service account policy from inside a response case. It ships through the Google Cloud partner integrations catalog.

Both integrations point in the same direction: identity telemetry and runtime enforcement reaching Google Cloud teams inside the tools they already run.

One platform for human, machine, and AI agent identities

AI agents do not operate in isolation. They share access paths with human users, service accounts, and other non-human identities, and they often create overlapping risk across all of them. A compromised or overprivileged agent can become a path to lateral movement, privilege escalation, or data exposure, and protecting the agent alone without visibility into the identities around it leaves gaps that attackers will find.

Silverfort brings AI agents into the same Identity Security Platform used to protect human and non-human identities across cloud and on-premises environments. Because those controls apply at runtime, they hold against both pressures – an agent drifting outside its approved scope, and an attacker moving at machine speed with credentials it should never have been able to use. Enterprises rarely run a single agentic AI platform, and enforcement extends across the wider ecosystem regardless of where agents run.

Availability

The Silverfort integration with Google Cloud’s Agent Gateway is now live. Organizations running AI agents on Google Cloud can get started without installing additional software or making code changes to existing workflows. Visibility and runtime protection begin on day one.

This is the beginning

Agentic AI is moving from experimentation to production faster than any enterprise technology in recent memory, and identity is where its security will be decided. Bringing runtime Identity Security to Agent Gateway is a significant step, and one of many we intend to take as the agentic ecosystem grows.

AI is accumulating security debt

Take, for example, agentic AI. Its adoption is accelerating rapidly and agents are operating across interconnected systems, giving threat actors more room to exploit vulnerabilities at the organizational level and across supply chains.

Full Text:
For the last several months, we’ve been busy talking to security teams and building answers to the AI-accelerated challenges that you’ve told us you’re facing. Among these are the overwhelming volume and velocity of alerts, exacerbated by attackers equipped with AI. The Hugging Face incident demonstrated another core challenge in the security operations center (SOC). Even if all of the signals are detected, that’s not enough, unless something connects them as part of a single attack. Combined, these problems force most teams to ration coverage by headcount, so the contents of the alert queue decide what gets attention, and the rest ages out unexamined. Spending time on proactive defenses then feels even more challenging.

Today, we’re giving you a peek at AlertZero, the new agentic layer of Elastic Security. AlertZero has a straightforward premise: put SOC teams on the path to the equivalent of inbox zero for alerts, with every alert answered. It does this by reducing the existing queue and the false positives that contribute to it, through high-volume correlation and enrichment, proposing actions, and then helping to create and tune detections.

AlertZero has agents, called Watches, each with one named job: Triage, Hunt, Detection, or Forensics. The Watches run on triggers and schedules to propose evidence-backed conclusions, called Proposed Actions, for approval, modification, escalation, or dismissal. Each Watch surfaces decisions to the analyst based on its autonomy level: manual, assisted, or supervised. Regardless of level, every consequential action is proposed to the analyst for approval.

AlertZero retains the same ″open by design″ philosophy as Elastic Security. You can use the model that works best for your team, including proprietary and open source models, with the same product and features, across Elastic Cloud, self-managed, or fully air-gapped.

We didn’t think of this overnight. AlertZero builds on three years of generative AI (GenAI) innovation in Elastic Security. Elastic AI Assistant started with conversational help in 2023. Attack Discovery extended that into a dedicated investigation task in 2024, connecting related alerts into an attack narrative. Elastic Agent Builder and security skills added agents that use tools and apply domain expertise, while Elastic Workflows supplies repeatable execution. AlertZero brings these capabilities together, tailored to the responsibilities of a SOC.

AlertZero Watches stay in their lane (and they handle it well)

Every Watch in AlertZero is directly aligned with the key responsibilities in the SOC, and their levels of autonomy are customizable. Within each Watch, Workers carry out specific tasks. For example, a Triage Worker runs Attack Discovery, which connects related alerts into attack narratives, while a Forensics Worker examines endpoint activity. Your team controls how much each Worker can do without human review, so you can tailor Watches to help your team in the places you most need it.

The upcoming technical preview introduces four Watches:

Watch name

What it helps your team do

Triage

Assesses alerts, connects related activity, and identifies findings that need attention.

Hunt

Uses threat research to look for evidence of attacks in the available telemetry.

Detection

Investigates noisy rules and coverage gaps and then prepares detection changes for review.

Forensics

Examines endpoint activity to establish what happened and to identify supported response actions.

A hunt can start from new threat research, and detection analysis can start from recurring false positives. Endpoint analysis can start from a finding that needs a closer look, and all of the Watches can run on triggers or a schedule. Watches don’t form a mandatory pipeline.

How AlertZero handles suspicious login sessions

The following example shows how the Triage and Forensics Hunts work together. We’re starting on the Proposed Actions page, where Watches awaiting human approval show their work before carrying out an action.

Proposed Actions are grouped by the type of action they’re waiting for. In this specific scenario, under Respond, an impossible-travel finding for an executive account, cfo@corp, has an endpoint-isolation action waiting for review. Before we even open this screen, the Triage Watch and Forensics Watch have already gathered the findings behind that recommendation.

Opening the item reveals the associated Investigation and its supporting evidence.

In this example, the account was active in Boston and then, 39 minutes later, it was active from a distant hosting network, using the same session identifier without a fresh multifactor authentication (MFA) event.

The endpoint findings add more context: an unsigned process accessing browser session material. If needed, we can examine how that process started and what it contacted, along with the time period covered. To see the full scope of the incident, there are the related alerts and affected entities, in addition to endpoint findings, in the same flyout. In this case, the pattern warrants investigating session replay. Virtual private network (VPN) use and proxies also need consideration, as does inaccurate geolocation.

From the Investigation’s conversation, we can ask these follow-up questions before deciding how to proceed: What did the account access after the suspicious sign-in? What would isolating the endpoint interrupt? These questions also prompt further analysis, and the existing findings are available as context.

In this scenario, the endpoint response is set to manual review. So, after checking the target, rationale, and likely impact, we can approve or decline the Proposed Action. An approval would trigger host isolation through Elastic Defend. The Investigation records the decision and the execution outcome separately for auditability.

When an Investigation (or set of Investigations) needs a coordinated and constrained response, an analyst can open an Escalation and link the relevant Investigations.

Teammates can discuss the evidence and, in the same conversation, ask an agent follow-up questions. They can also opt to never invoke an agent in particularly sensitive situations.

Beyond alert triage: What else does AlertZero do?

Reducing the alert queue by handling the correlation and enrichment at scale is one part of the solution. On the other side of things, we’re helping with the work that happens when nothing is on fire.

A head start on your hunt

For threat hunting, the Hunt Watch:

Continuously observes your environment.

Maps observed technologies and exposures to relevant threats.

Proposes hunts, findings, coverage improvements, or escalations.

Its core purpose is to answer the question Is there evidence of this threat in my environment?, without requiring you to provoke the hunt or feed the intel.

The Hunt Watch gets you started with threat research, even when no detection alert has been fired. It relates that research to the environment and available telemetry and searches for relevant indicators. It also examines supporting behavior. The findings identify what was searched and what was found.

Turning false positives and coverage gaps into rule changes

To improve your environment-specific defenses, hunt findings can inform the Detection Watch by looking at whether existing rules would detect the behavior.

Suppose a legitimate administrative tool repeatedly triggers a rule. The closure itself is useful feedback, but someone still has to connect several decisions to a common cause in the rule. This is how false-positive closures provide another input for the Detection Watch to contextualize. The Watch reviews the alert examples and existing logic and then prepares a proposed change, like an exception, with the supporting diagnosis. From there, a detection engineer can assess whether a narrow exception fits the benign activity while preserving detection of malicious use of the same tool.

As an example, the Watch would run an Elasticsearch Query Language (ES|QL) query like this:

Once the Watch reviews the rules’ rankings based on their recently closed false positives, it identifies those with high counts to investigate further. A high count doesn’t necessarily prove that the rule is defective, but the analysis needs to inspect the examples and their closure rationale, because an incorrect false-positive label can otherwise become an incorrect exclusion.

In this example, the Detection Watch’s Rule Tuning Worker is set to manual. After the analyst authorizes the analysis, the resulting Proposed Action brings together the diagnosis, the motivating alerts, the existing logic, the proposed logic, and backtest results. That gives a detection engineer an actual change to assess and the evidence used to construct it.

With the proposal, we can see that the five sample false positives no longer match the revised query.

We can open the Proposed Action to review the change and ask follow-up questions in the linked Investigation, such as What other activity would this exclusion suppress? Because this backtest only covers benign samples, the analyst still needs to validate detection of known malicious activity through the team’s existing testing process before approving. If it’s approved, the change is applied; if it’s declined, the rule is unchanged.

You can decide how much to delegate

You choose which Watches run and how far each goes, with autonomy configurable per Worker. We’ve built this into AlertZero because no two security teams are organized the same way. Some run tiers, some run pods, many have no detection engineer, and most cannot staff nights. Regardless of team structure, autonomy also is configurable because different jobs carry different risks, like assessing an alert versus responding on an endpoint. You can delegate routine analysis while choosing more cautiously when a host may be affected. As an example, the Triage Watch Worker runs Attack Discovery, while a Forensics Watch Worker performs endpoint analysis. Each runs as an Elastic Workflow, calling Agent Builder agents and skills for analysis.

For true-positive or inconclusive Attack Discovery assessments, manual review lets the analyst decide whether to close an Investigation or request endpoint analysis. In supervised operation, a true-positive assessment can continue into endpoint analysis automatically. An inconclusive assessment still needs a person's decision.

Endpoint analysis has its own control. Manual operation presents supported response actions for review. Supervised operation is designed to permit host isolation, process termination, and process suspension without an additional approval for each action. Detection changes continue to require approval. Teams can therefore automate one part of the sequence while retaining review of another.

Every alert is answered, and every decision is yours

As AI that helps move an investigation forward, AlertZero connects work that too often stops at a handoff. The evidence gathered during triage can guide endpoint analysis and support a response decision. It can also give teammates a place to continue the investigation. Teams choose what to delegate and where their judgment is needed.

To know when future AlertZero news is published, sign up for updates. AlertZero will be available soon to all users of Elastic Security.

Glossary

AlertZero: The agentic layer of Elastic Security, connecting alert triage, threat hunting, detection engineering, and endpoint forensics.

Watch: A grouping of automated tasks around a security responsibility. The initial four are Triage, Hunt, Detection, and Forensics.

Worker: A defined task implemented as a workflow in Elastic Workflows, using agents and skills to produce findings, evidence, and supported actions.

Proposed Actions: Recommended changes with supporting evidence and rationale, presented for approval where review is required.

Investigation: The shared record for a line of inquiry, bringing together findings, affected entities, evidence, and Proposed Actions.

Escalation: A conversation that a person creates to coordinate work around linked Investigations. Teammates can discuss evidence and ask agents questions; visibility can be public or private.

Autonomy setting: A per-Worker control over how much work can proceed without review. Its behavior depends on the task.

Consequential action: An operation that changes the environment, such as isolating a host or editing a rule.

Elastic Defend: Elastic's endpoint security capability, providing supported endpoint response actions.

Attack Discovery: A capability that connects related alerts into suspected attacks. The Triage Watch uses it to open an Investigation for each identified attack.

Elastic Agent Builder, Elastic Workflows: Extensible building blocks for Watches: Agent Builder provides agents, tools, and skills; Elastic Workflows coordinates execution.

Title: Introducing Wiz AI SAST: Application Security that Understands Your Code and Your Infrastructure
Context: We’re excited to announce that Wiz AI SAST is available as a Public Preview capability, bringing frontier-grade vulnerability discovery to all Wiz Code customers
Full Text:
We’re excited to announce that Wiz AI SAST is available as a Public Preview capability, bringing frontier-grade vulnerability discovery to all Wiz Code customers.

AI models have become highly adept at finding complex flaws in application code that traditional scanners often miss. Security teams historically addressed this gap with manual reviews and quarterly pentesting, but neither of those approaches scale in a world where code is written and exploited at machine speed.

Wiz AI SAST addresses this gap by analyzing how your application actually behaves to uncover a broader range of weaknesses (CWEs) that typically go undetected by rules-based scanners. It's powered by the Atlas harness we shared earlier this year, grounded in Wiz Research, and continuously refined by our investments in AI security.

Code findings are correlated with what is actually running in production on the Wiz Security Graph, so teams instantly understand which vulnerabilities matter most. Prioritized findings flow through the existing policy, ownership, and remediation workflows AppSec teams already use, making AI-powered vulnerability detection part of your existing program rather than another tool to manage.

As a core part of our AI Threat Readiness Framework, Wiz AI SAST complements a broader portfolio of solutions designed to help organizations stay ahead of cyberthreats in the AI era.

Frontier Grade Code Analysis without the Overhead

Running AI code scanning in production takes far more than a capable model. Teams have to build a harness that turns that model into a capable security researcher, evaluate new models as they ship, and manage the lifecycle of findings into security workflows. Done in-house, it requires a significant, ongoing investment from skilled security and engineering teams. Wiz AI SAST handles all of that out-of-the-box so organizations can operationalize AI code scanning quickly to improve their risk posture.

A Harness Backed by Research and Results

Wiz AI SAST shares the same underlying technology as Atlas, a research initiative we shared earlier this year. At the time, Atlas held the number one spot on CyberGym and uncovered more than 200 vulnerabilities in widely used open source software.

We continuously tune our harness with learnings from real-world vulnerability research, attacker techniques, and scanning across Wiz's cloud security footprint. Organizations benefit from our expertise without having to build and maintain the complex AI infrastructure required for security specific use cases.

Model Selection Driven by Continuous Benchmarking

Our work on the Cyber Model Arena shows that AI security performance isn't a property of the model alone. It depends on the model and harness together. That makes evaluation a moving target: every new model release means retesting every pairing against real-world security tasks.

As an AI vendor-agnostic platform, we continuously run these evaluations and swap the strongest—and most efficient—model into the AI SAST harness. This includes cutting edge cybermodels made available to us through our partnership with Google DeepMind.

For security teams, the value is simple: you don’t need to constantly track new model releases, benchmark them against security tasks, or decide which model to use. We handle that complexity behind the scenes, ensuring your code and applications are always scanned with the best model.

Turning Non-Deterministic AI into a Scalable Security Program

Delivering an enterprise-grade AI AppSec program requires managing the full lifecycle of vulnerability discovery, starting with deciding what to scan. AI code analysis is resource intensive and not every asset requires the investment of AI reasoning. Using Mika AI, security teams can prioritize the critical repositories that warrant AI code scanning by drawing on context such as cloud exposure, access to sensitive data, and business criticality.

Once those prioritized scans are running, Wiz addresses the next phase of the lifecycle: the outputs. Because Large Language Models (LLMs) are inherently non-deterministic, they can generate different results from one run to the next. This creates a major operational challenge for security teams who need consistency in findings.

To solve this we supplement the AI scan engine with automated lifecycle management to maintain finding states across scans:

Retest: Before scanning for new risks, the engine re-examines existing findings to confirm they're still valid. If the code has been fixed, the finding is automatically marked resolved.

Deduplicate: Rather than matching on line numbers or file paths, the engine correlates new findings with existing ones using security context and code semantics. Even if the AI changes a bug's title or description, our AI SAST recognizes the underlying root cause and reconciles it into a single, stable finding.

Wiz handles this lifecycle between scans automatically, ensuring teams work with stable findings that can be assigned, tracked, remediated, and closed—not a new, disconnected set of AI outputs after every scan.

As a result customers get the deep detection benefits of AI without giving up the predictable workflows they expect from enterprise security tools. By eliminating the manual burden of managing non-determinism, this built-in continuity dramatically reduces the Total Cost of Ownership (TCO) of AI-powered security.

Click through the feature tour

See how Wiz AI SAST works

Visibility into a New Class of CWEs

Wiz AI SAST extends detection coverage into the logic-based vulnerabilities that have always been hardest to catch, like broken access control, flawed input validation, and misapplied cryptography. Finding them requires a semantic understanding of what the code is supposed to do, which is something AI does exceptionally well.

A practical example can be found below. Wiz AI SAST detected an Insecure Direct Object Reference (IDOR) flaw in an E-commerce basket endpoint, where any authenticated user could read another user's cart by changing the ID in the URL. Rules based engines would miss this type of risk because the syntax of the code is fine but it's the missing ownership check that makes it exploitable.

The practical takeaway for AppSec teams is that AI analysis doesn’t replace rules based scanning completely, but rather it extends it. Deterministic scanning provides fast, cost-effective coverage for syntax based flaws, while AI SAST adds the deep reasoning needed to catch intent-dependent flaws like the IDOR above. Together, they give AppSec teams broader coverage of risk across the entire application attack surface.

Prioritize Exploitable Risks with Code-to-Infrastructure Context

The best AI models in the world are ultimately limited by their access to relevant context. A model evaluating code in a vacuum is blind to how that application actually operates in the real world.

By grounding our AI SAST engine in the Wiz Security Graph, the model investigates your code with full awareness of your infrastructure, identity configurations, and runtime environment. This context serves two critical purposes:

Uncovering Hidden Risk: It allows the AI to discover complex vulnerabilities that only exist at the intersection of application logic and infrastructure flaws that standalone AI code scanners cannot detect.

Prioritizing True Attack Paths: It drastically reduces triage fatigue by correlating code weaknesses with additional context to surface critical attack paths that matter most for remediation.

That same deep context is what allows our Red Agent to validate exploitability from the outside in, testing these AI-discovered findings against your live environment exactly the way an attacker would.

Remediate at Machine Speed with the Green Agent

Detecting and validating risk at machine speed only pays off if remediation keeps up. The Wiz Green Agent investigates the underlying findings and builds a remediation plan grounded in the full context of your code, pipeline, infrastructure, and runtime, going beyond the generic guidance a standalone model produces.

It pinpoints the right owner, maps the steps to fix the root cause, and can even share context with an AI coding agent like Claude Code to carry out the fix in code. And with Wiz Workflows, teams can turn Green Agent’s intelligence into multi-step automated response chains tailored to their DevSecOps playbooks.

Get Started

In the AI era, the best form of defense is to use AI on ourselves before threat actors can. Wiz AI SAST gives defenders a scalable solution to apply that philosophy against application code. But, it’s just one component of our broader vision for Agentic Code Security where specialized AI agents work alongside security teams to autonomously investigate, prioritize, and remediate risk across the entire AI development lifecycle.

Wiz AI SAST is available now in Public Preview. If you’re an existing Wiz Code customer, get started by visiting our documentation. If you’re new to Wiz, request a demo to experience frontier-grade vulnerability discovery first hand.

Title: Beyond Triage: How the Aurora Agentic SOC Enhances the Concierge Experience
Context: Curated by the world’s largest commercial SOC based on real-world attacks, emerging threats, and observed adversary behavior
Full Text:
A lot of the current conversation about agentic SOCs is about triage. Faster detection, faster investigation, alerts resolved in minutes instead of hours. When we set out to build the Aurora® Agentic SOC, we didn’t just want to make triage faster. We fundamentally re-engineered our SOC to strengthen every job it does, and enhancing the Concierge Experience™ for our customers was a key part of that.

Arctic Wolf’s SOC, both before and after the Aurora Agentic SOC era, has always centered on two complementary teams. The Triage Security Team investigates and responds to alerts around the clock, containing threats in real time. The Concierge Security Team, and the Concierge Experience they help deliver, focuses on the proactive side of cybersecurity, giving customers a dedicated team that knows their environment and provides guidance to help strengthen their security posture.

Ask customers why they chose Arctic Wolf, and why they stay, and you’ll always get a variety of answers, but the Concierge Experience consistently appears near the top of both lists. That isn’t a coincidence. It comes from a relationship built over time. A deep understanding of each customer’s business. The ability to act as an extension of their team rather than a vendor operating at a distance. The best version of that relationship still depends on people, as AI’s role is to clear the administrative work out of their way so they can spend that time on customers instead.

Our Concierge Security Team is in constant communication with customers, learning about changes that shape their environment: a leadership transition, a new facility, a product launch, or an acquisition. Along the way, they learn which systems and users are truly critical to the business, and which only appear that way on paper.

In a single word, that relationship is built on context.

Context is understanding what matters to a specific customer. It allows analysts and the Aurora Agentic SOC to distinguish activity that is normal for one organization from activity that would be unusual for another. It’s one reason Aurora MDR customers, on average, receive less than one alert per day. Not because alerts are filtered away, but because investigations are informed by an understanding of what is actually meaningful for that customer.

Building context that detailed isn’t easy. When we built the Aurora Agentic SOC, we took the opportunity to embed customer context even deeper into the Concierge Experience. Through the Aurora Agentic SOC, Arctic Wolf uses AI in four distinct ways to help customers and Concierge Security Teams spend less time on administration and more time focused on what matters most: building a resilient business in the age of AI.

How AI Helps Concierge Security Teams Focus on What Matters Most

1. Research Before All Touchpoints

Customer profile, history, and recent activity in one view.

Ahead of a customer touchpoint, the Aurora Agentic SOC assembles the context an analyst needs. What’s changed since the last conversation? Which action items remain open? What surfaced in the most recent SPiDR review? Any recent alerts or investigations that may be relevant to the discussion?

Instead of spending the first few minutes of a meeting rebuilding context, analysts start informed and prepared. The conversation begins with decisions rather than a recap.

2. Context Captured During the Call

Live transcripts surfaced with questions and action items.

Live transcription surfaces questions and action items as they come up, helping ensure important details aren’t lost after the conversation ends.

The more important capability is what happens to business context shared during the discussion. That context doesn’t remain buried in meeting notes. It becomes structured context connected to the customer’s environment and available to future investigations and recommendations.

When a related alert appears weeks later, analysts and the Aurora Agentic SOC have more than a transcript to reference. They have context that helps explain why the activity matters.

3. Follow-Through After the Call

Meeting outcomes automatically captured and organized.

Decisions and action items are automatically captured and routed when a meeting concludes, for both Arctic Wolf teams and customer stakeholders.

This is especially valuable during SPiDR reviews, where recommendations often require action over time. Automated follow-ups help keep that work moving, highlight overdue items, and create accountability around agreed-upon next steps.

Instead of recommendations becoming another list to revisit later, progress remains visible and measurable.

4. Guidance Built on Scale

Risk assessments and recommendations tailored to each customer.

Customer context is powerful on its own. The Aurora Agentic SOC makes it even more valuable.

The Aurora Agentic SOC combines customer-specific context with insights derived from Arctic Wolf’s broad security operations experience, helping Concierge Security Teams identify emerging trends, common gaps, and the security improvements that deliver meaningful impact for the customers they serve. The result is guidance that is both highly personalized and informed by a much broader view of real-world security operations.

Reviews become more strategic, helping customers understand where they stand, where risk remains, and where to focus next.

Call it a feedback loop. Every interaction makes the Aurora Agentic SOC more informed about a customer’s business. The context gathered before, during, and after each conversation carries forward, improving the relevance of future recommendations and helping the SOC distinguish normal activity from potential threats more quickly.

Over time, that knowledge compounds. The Aurora Agentic SOC experience becomes increasingly specific to each customer, strengthening recommendations, accelerating investigations, and helping analysts make decisions with greater confidence. The result is a Concierge Experience that grows more valuable over time, helping customers make better security decisions faster and build a more resilient business.
